Hua Qi, or American Flags Made in China: The Crossroads of Nationalism and Capitalism
From the halls of Congress to the local American Legion, from high-brow magazines to local newspapers, American flags made in China have captured the contempt, the concurrence, or simply the curiosity of the American people. Since September 11, 2001, the American flag made in China has been used as a way to talk about a variety of concerns, including China's human and religious rights violations and its communist government. Most significantly, however, the anxiety about American flags made in China reflects a palpable sense of anxiety about the U.S. economy and its place in the world. Rather than adjudicating the advantages and disadvantages of globalization, as the much of the current literature attempts to do, I analyze the rhetoric surrounding a particularly "loaded" cultural artifact as it circulates through Chinese and American cultures. I conclude that although, in the abstract, globalization and the nation-state can be compatible, if not complementary, the discourses about and images of American flags made in China suggest that nationalism—a commitment to the nation-state as well as hostility toward another nation—is animating much of the opinion in the United States. The implications of this anxiety will continue to influence U.S. economic and trade policy within the Sino-American relationship and, ultimately, how Americans see the United States' role in the world.
Fields: American Studies; History
Concepts: American flag; made in China; nationalism; globalization; US-China relations; post-9/11 patriotism; economic anxiety; cultural artifact; material culture; consumer goods; manufacturing outsourcing; political rhetoric; Chinese export industry

Rural Worlds Gained: The Migration of People from Southeast Missouri to Northeast Louisiana and Northeast Texas during the Mid-Twentieth Century
In the late 1950s and early '60s, amidst an overcrowding agricultural landscape, a throng of farmers from Southeast Missouri and Central Arkansas seized opportunity to better their lives and continue their farming tradition for future generations of their families. They migrated to Northeast Louisiana where land was being cleared and new cropland was available in abundance; they overcame numerous hardships; and in the end they transformed Northeast Louisiana into the thriving agricultural region it is today, preserving both their way of life and a small piece of the rural ethos that is so prevalent in the American imagination.
Fields: History; American Studies

Public vs. Private Space: The Roman Cubiculum
The Roman villa had a very different function than its contemporary counterpart since it served as both a country retreat and as a place where much work and public entertaining took place. The villa was divided into a public and private sector, which were both clearly delineated based on the status of a visitor. The private sector of a house is more difficult to analyze due to a lack of information about the daily activities, which occurred in restricted rooms such as cubicula or bedrooms. With the help of an Undergraduate Research Grant, I have compared the frescoes of three aristocratic cubicula around Pompeii in an attempt to discover more about the daily life of Romans in the first centuries BC and AD. In doing this analysis it became clear that the typologies used by archaeologists in the past are outdated and they do allow us to understand how versatile rooms in Roman villas were. The frescoes and architectural elements of these three cubicula reveal that “bedrooms” were in fact used for a variety of activities such as sleeping but also dining, reading, studying and small parties. The typologies imposed by archaeologist in the past have been detrimental to the study of Roman villas and this study of “bedrooms” based on décor reveals how multifaceted spaces could be.
Fields: Classics; Art History; Archaeology
Concepts: Roman villa; cubiculum; Pompeii; Second Style wall painting; frescoes; Roman domestic space; public and private space; Roman daily life; Campania; Roman art; room function; household archaeology

Buried in the Benta Valley: Discovery and Analysis of Bronze Age Burial Sites of Hungary's Vatya Culture
In burials lie the transition between life and death. The placement of the dead cross-culturally and throughout history often reflects idealized social stratifications, distributions of wealth and control of resources. In Hungary, Bronze Age cemeteries have been located near tells – gradually built up mounds or hills covering successive remains of ancient communities. At one such tell discovered near Százhalombatta, Hungary, the mortuary practices of the Vatya who occupied the area, and what those practices tell us about this Bronze Age people, remain largely unexplored. This research project focuses primarily on identifying and investigating the relationships between the cemeteries and settlements of the Vatya culture during the Middle Bronze Age in the Benta Valley, Hungary. Using existing research on Middle Bronze Age cemeteries, maps of the Benta Valley, and the current work on settlements conducted by the Benta Valley Project, I created a model to identify Vatya cemeteries in relation to settlements through topographic patterns and survey based on a Vatya burial site signature. Maps created using ArcGIS programs, that include both Middle Bronze Age settlement patterns and density with MBA cemetery patterns, will form a visual representation to develop spatial and topographic relationships of settlement size and location with cemetery size and location in the Benta Valley, to analyze further how the hierarchy of the settlements relates to the hierarchy of the cemeteries. Both located at high elevations transposed across streambeds, Vatya settlements of the dead reflect the settlements of the living with some distortion.
Fields: Anthropology; Archaeology
Concepts: Bronze Age; Vatya culture; Hungary; Százhalombatta; Benta Valley; tell settlements; mortuary archaeology; burials; cemeteries; social stratification; settlement patterns; European prehistory; Timothy Earle; landscape archaeology

Michel Foucault and Museums
In the late sixties the French philosopher Michel Foucault was contracted to write a book about the painter Eduard Manet. Foucault often used examples from art in his philosophy but rarely addressed art itself. This book on Manet, some scholars argue, was to articulate a philosophy of art for Foucault. However, Foucault never finished the book and destroyed all his written materials that related to this work. The only remnant of this work is a recorded lecture delivered in Tunisia in 1971. My research analyzed these recordings from Tunis. Although they are only a small extract from a larger project, they still contain unique ideas about art. By taking these ideas from the lectures and placing them in the context of Foucault’s larger oeuvre, my project developed into a discussion about the relationship between art and museums. To expand on these concepts about museums, I investigated France’s newest art museum, the Musée du Quai Branly. This museum opened in the summer of 2006. From the day it was first proposed, this museum has been a source of controversy in France. Critics, academics, and politicians of all stripes have lambasted it, while others held it up as a model art museum. I examine the controversy in light of the Tunis lectures and Foucault’s thoughts on Manet. In the end I use the Musée du Quai Branly as case study for discussing Foucault’s unique ideas and in turn use the Foucault to provide new perspective on contemporary French culture.
Fields: Philosophy; Art Theory
Concepts: Michel Foucault; Édouard Manet; Tunis lecture; philosophy of art; museums; aesthetics; modern painting; French philosophy; continental philosophy; spectator; institutional critique; Penelope Deutscher

CK2 - A Novel Link Between Fragile X Mental Retardation and Circadian Rhythms
A loss of function mutation in the human Fragile X Mental Retardation gene (fmr) is associated with a wide range of clinical abnormalities, including sleep defects. Remarkably, a homologous mutation in the Drosophila gene dfmr results similarly in poor circadian rhythms and altered sleep phenotypes. My interest is in what links fmr to sleep and the circadian clock. In order to understand this link, we take advantage of Drosophila and its fmr homologue as our model. My first project investigates a proposed interaction between CKII, a gene associated with the circadian clock, and dfmr. To investigate the possibility of this interaction, I have performed a variety of molecular and genetic experiments. My second project is a screen for enhancers and suppressors of the dfmr mutant phenotype. Mutant dfmr lines are further mutagenized and tested for resultant changes in behavioral phenotype. Lines accruing mutations that enhance or suppress the dfmr phenotype are saved and their mutations mapped. These mutations may help to identify pathways connecting dfmr to the clock, and in doing so help to identify the essential pathways through which fmr gives rise to its variety of symptoms.
Fields: Neuroscience; Genetics

Investigation of Nuclear Pore Complex Proteins in Gene Recruitment
DNA in the eukaryotic nucleus exhibits spatial organization that can rapidly change in response to transcriptional and developmental cues. Studies in yeast and other organisms have found that certain inducible genes are dynamically recruited to the nuclear periphery when transcriptionally active. These findings suggest that proximity of the DNA to the nuclear periphery could play a role in regulating gene expression. Therefore, a fundamental understanding of how genes are recruited to the nuclear periphery can shed insight into how cells target DNA to a specific nuclear location and the functional implications of this controlled targeting event. We are using the yeast GAL1 gene as a model system to dissect the molecular requirements of gene recruitment to the nuclear periphery. Using a candidate approach, we have classified four broad categories of non-essential proteins that might be involved in recruiting genes to the nuclear periphery: which include 1) nuclear pore components, 2) chromatin modifying proteins, 3) nucleoplasmic motor proteins, and 4) other nuclear periphery proteins. Using a gene deletion technique based on homologous recombination, we have generated a collection of null mutants and analyzed the requirement of these protein candidates in GAL1 gene recruitment. By means of a quantitative chromatin localization assay, we have found a subset of nuclear pore components and chromatin modifying proteins to be required for gene recruitment to the nuclear periphery. These results suggest that the nuclear pore complex is the site to which active genes are recruited and that chromatin modifications may play a key role in targeting of active genes to the nuclear periphery.
Fields: Molecular Biology; Cell Biology
Concepts: nuclear pore complex; nucleoporins; gene recruitment; nuclear periphery; GAL1; Saccharomyces cerevisiae; budding yeast; nuclear organization; gene positioning; transcriptional regulation; chromatin; Jason Brickner

Understanding the Regulation of DNA Localization
The nucleus is a highly organized structure composed of distinct chromosomal territories. The spatial arrangement of DNA can dramatically influence the transcriptional state of genes in eukaryotic cells. The nuclear periphery was once associated exclusively with silenced genes. However, recent studies find that many genes are actively recruited to the nuclear envelope upon expression, and in some cases this is necessary to promote maximal transcription levels. This inducible association with the nuclear periphery is known as gene recruitment. The INO1 gene in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is one gene that undergoes gene recruitment. Transcription of INO1 is negatively regulated by Opi1. When Opi1 is bound to the INO1 promoter, transcription is repressed and the gene is nucleoplasimic; Opi1 dissociation leads to INO1 activation and recruitment to the periphery. We hypothesize that Opi1 is also involved in regulating gene recruitment of INO1. We have identified an element within the INO1 promoter, known as the Gene Recruitment Sequence (GRS), both necessary and sufficient to target DNA to the nuclear periphery. Integrating the GRS at a distant site in the genome causes targeting of that site to the periphery constitutively. Similarly, cells lacking Opi1 demonstrate constitutive targeting of INO1. Thus, Opi1 may also function as a negative regulator of gene recruitment. I find that targeting Opi1 near either of its two endogenous binding sites in the INO1 promoter is sufficient to repress gene recruitment. These results indicate that Opi1 is involved in regulating gene recruitment and may do so by interrupting the GRS signal.
Fields: Molecular Biology; Cell Biology
Concepts: gene recruitment; INO1; Opi1; nuclear periphery; nuclear envelope; Saccharomyces cerevisiae; yeast genetics; transcriptional repression; chromosome territories; DNA localization; promoter elements; Jason Brickner

Characterizing the Tryptophan-41 Residue of Influenza M2 Protein
Despite medical advances, the influenza virus still results in 36,000 deaths per year in the United States. This has caused researchers to strive to discover alternative strategies in combating the virus. One strategy involves inhibiting the crucial M2 proton channel protein located in the virus membrane. M2 activation occurs when surrounding pH decreases, as in an endosome. The lower pH results in M2 permitting proton conductance, lowering the pH within the virion interior. This in turn causes the release of influenza RNA from the viral membrane protein and allows the RNA to diffuse into the cytoplasm, infecting the cell. Currently, the M2 activation mechanism is unknown. Two residues, His-37 and Trp-41, have been determined to be necessary for M2 function. By understanding how even one of these residues changes conformation when M2 is activated, new methods for disrupting M2 activation can be developed. The indole side chain of Trp-41 is inherently fluorescent. Dyes that undergo quenching by Trp-41 can be placed at particular locations on the protein and the amount of emission quenching can be measured. Quenching directly correlates to the distance between the Trp-41 and the dye and changes in the amount of quenching will show the movement of Trp-41 during activation. This experiment has been conducted from the ecto-domain of M2 and repeating them from the cytoplasmic domain will allow for comparison. By using fluorescence, Trp-41 conformation change during activation and accessibility will be observed. From this new ideas can be developed on inhibiting M2, particularly at Trp-41, and combating the virus.
Fields: Biophysics; Virology
Concepts: influenza; M2 proton channel; ion channels; tryptophan-41; histidine-37; channel gating; pH activation; fluorescence spectroscopy; viral uncoating; antiviral targets; amantadine; Lawrence Pinto

Smooth Muscle Myosin Heavy Chain (SMMHC) Structure, Function and Role in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (SMMHC) is a protein affected by inv(16), which fuses its C-terminal coiled-coil domain with a majority of the core binding factor b (CBFb) transcription factor. inv(16) is the most common chromosomal inversion found in gene karyotypes of patients diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). SMMHC, a component of a contractile protein complex found in smooth muscle cells of various organs of the body, exists as a bipolar dimer by way of a C-terminal coiled-coil and a globular N-terminal head with ATPase activity. The focus of this project has been to study the C-terminal domain (CTD) of SMMHC using biophysical methods. Here we analyze the nature of the SMMHC domain and provide some insight into the structure of the multimerization domain. NMR analysis of 13C and/or 15N labeled SMMHC suggests that the coiled-coil has a natively unfolded tail. The remaining residues form a rigid structured coil. The structure of the rod-like coil and oligomerization state of SMMHC was studied using analytical ultracentrifugation and crystallography. Velocity sedmientation experiments have been run at varying salt concentrations of 100 mM (low salt), 150 mM (physiological), and 200 mM or 300 mM KCl (high salt) because SMMHC demonstrates a strong salt dependence in vitro in order to multimerize. Unexpectedly, analysis showed that at lower ionic strengths, SMMHC may exist in several heterogeneous dimer conformations or as an aggregated filament. Current models suggest that filaments form as ordered anti-parallel dimers, which aggregate into tetramers, octomers, and so on, but we suggest that formation of filaments may not be as straightforward.
Fields: Structural Biology; Biochemistry

Monitoring Aggregation and Characterizing the Effects of Aggregation Suppression on Toxicity in C. elegans
Aggregation of misfolded proteins is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative diseases, including Amyotropic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and the polyglutamine (polyQ) disorders. PolyQ disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of a glutamine repetitive tract that induce protein misfolding and aggregation. Aggregates in familial form of ALS arise from unstable, mutant Cu,Zn-superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) proteins that tend to form oligomers and filamentous arrays. Although aggregates have been observed to accumulate in parallel with the clinical course of these neurodegenerative diseases, studies to date have been unable to definitively establish if aggregation is causal, consequential, or incidental to neurotoxicity. A genome-wide RNA interference screen identified 67 suppressors of visible aggregates in polyQ and SOD1 C. elegans models. This study characterizes the consequences of polyQ aggregation suppression on toxicity. Animal movement, characterized by speed and coordination, serves as a readout for organism toxicity, and automated tracking software has been developed to this end. Motility assays suggest that the presence of visible aggregates is uncoupled from toxicity, lending credence to the hypothesis that polyQ-induced toxicity is not directly caused by aberrant protein-protein interactions facilitated by end-stage aggregates. A better understanding of the aggregation process, its regulation, and its link to toxicity will provide insight into the mechanisms by which neurodegenerative disorders are triggered.
Fields: Cell Biology; Neuroscience
Concepts: protein aggregation; misfolded proteins; polyglutamine; Huntington's disease; ALS; SOD1; C. elegans; RNAi screen; proteotoxicity; neurodegeneration; proteostasis; Richard Morimoto

Estrogen Mechanism in Thermoregulation
Hot flashes commonly occur during menopause – a physiological phenomenon in which women cease to ovulate, and therefore lose the production of endogenous estrogen. It is hypothesized that this loss of estrogen causes the change in thermoregulation, which results in the experience of hot flashes. Thermoregulation takes place primarily in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus via the activity of temperature sensitive neurons. We aim to uncover the mechanism by which estrogen alters the sensitivity of these neurons. We have found that estrogen potentially acts through the modification of activity of the potassium channels known as background-leak or K2P channels. Because these channels can alter the electrical activity of a neuron and because it has been shown that they respond to changes in temperature, we hypothesize that K2P channels mediate the effects of estrogen on thermoregulation. Our experiments have found that the effect of these channels of thermoregulation does indeed differ between animals with estrogen versus animals that lack estrogen. Furthermore, we are working to discover what type of estrogen receptor is involved in this mechanism. The classical model of estrogen receptor is a ligand-activated transcription factor that mediates transcriptional events in response to estrogen. However, because these transcriptional events require a time period of several hours to days, whereas we have found that estrogen can alter thermoregulation within less than an hour, we have, therefore, turned our attention to a third potential estrogen receptor, GPR30, and are currently studying the possibility of its role in the hot flash mechanism.
Fields: Neuroscience; Physiology
Concepts: hot flashes; menopause; estrogen; thermoregulation; preoptic area; hypothalamus; thermosensitive neurons; K2P channels; two-pore domain potassium channels; neuroendocrinology; women's health

Asymmetric Ring-Opening of Meso-Epoxides with Alcohols Catalyzed by Chiral Aluminum Complexes
Every living organism is composed of molecules, big and small, with specific chiral orientations that are intricately involved in that organism's ability to control its life processes. Nearly every biochemical process in the human body is associated with specific chiral molecules. As a result, many prescription drugs must possess a particular chiral orientation to be effective. Therefore, great care is taken during the synthesis of these molecules to control their chirality. However, this is not an easy task, and the difficulty in making a chirally pure drug is partially responsible for the rising cost of prescription drugs and health insurance. Therefore, any synthetic advances that can ease this burden or eliminate steps in the manufacturing of chiral drugs have a very high potential to reduce the cost of healthcare. Although synthetic organic chemists have developed numerous methods to control the chirality of a particular molecule, they have not been uniformly successful. To enhance the chiral purity of a particular drug intermediate, expensive starting materials are often required, reaction conditions must be carefully controlled, and an extensive product purification must be carried out. As such, synthetic approaches that can yield chirally pure products without such intensive requirements would be very valuable. To this end, I aim to develop an efficient synthesis of chirally pure B-hydroxyethers, an important class of intermediates for the pharmaceutical and fine chemicals industries, from non-chiral starting materials. This conversion can be achieved under mild reaction conditions in the presence of a highly active but easily accessible aluminum-based catalyst.
Fields: Chemistry

Roman Children's Funerary Monuments
Children’s funerary monuments provide insight into the ways in which children were viewed and represented in Roman society. Understanding children’s funerary portraiture is especially useful in this regard, as portraits of children often differ significantly from those of adults. In their respective studies of Roman funerary altars and children’s sarcophagi, Diana Kleiner and Janet Huskinson have discussed broader themes of portraiture in funerary iconography. My research examines a particular subset of these depictions - iconographic allusions to divinity in children’s monuments. I suggest that children are often represented with elements of the divine not only to suggest hope for continued life after death, but also as shorthand for unattained stages of adulthood. In this paradox of representation, children can be commemorated in immortal play alongside divine beings, but also in mature roles as an adult god. For this presentation, I will focus upon monuments of girls as Venus and Diana as well as children represented as putti or “baby cupids.” These portrait depictions blend traditional religious and cultural attributes of the divinity represented, such as sexuality or chastity, with allusions to the social norms of adult monuments. In this way, monuments depicting children as divinities emphasize both the child’s young age at death and the adult attainments and characteristics they never lived to fulfill. These depictions can also suggest a class-consciousness, as former slaves often commemorated their free-born children in a manner which suggested the increased social and legal opportunities that their parents lacked.
Fields: Classics; Art History
Concepts: Roman funerary art; children in antiquity; sarcophagi; funerary altars; portraiture; iconography; divinity; death and commemoration; childhood in ancient Rome; Roman art

X-Ray binaries are double star systems consisting of a dense compact object, such as a neutron star or black hole, in tight orbit around another star. Stellar material is transferred from the star onto the compact object, creating extremely bright X-Ray emissions, which are easily detected by modern X-Ray telescopes such as the Chandra X-Ray Observatory. Here, I will show theoretical models of the X-Ray binary population resulting from a large burst of star formation activity, focusing on activity between 25-60 million years after star formation. During this interval, the X-Ray binary population is highly impacted by an event known as an electron-capture supernovae, in which electrons merge with the heavy elements inside a massive star to create explosions significantly different from traditional iron core-collapse supernovae. While electron-capture systems may form a significant portion of the observed neutron star population, existing theoretical models dispute both the percentage of systems, which will undergo electron-capture, as well as the energetics of the electron-capture process. I will show how X-Ray binary observations uniquely allow us to constrain the population of electron-capture supernovae and use accepted values of these parameters to explain the overabundance of X-Ray binary sources in the Small Magellanic Clouds.

In fact, I observed a conflict between traditional values and Western values in almost all areas of Anlo-Ewe culture. It is my hope that the findings of my research will not only improve the Western understanding of Anlo-Ewe music, but will also inspire other Westerners to consider the traditional Anlo-Ewe view of time as a healthy alternative to our own narrow, stress-inducing views of time.

Visualization of Individual mRNA Transcripts in Single Living Yeast Cells
Divergent gene pairs—two genes oriented “back-to-back” along a stretch of a chromosome— uniquely focus attention on a fundamental problem in gene regulation. How does a gene regulatory protein obeying only the laws of physics “know” which gene it is supposed to be regulating? Traditional studies of transcriptional regulation—how a gene gets turned on or off—measure average values across cell populations, but do not answer this question. For example, a study might find that each cell in a given population possesses on average 0.7 mRNA molecules of a given gene. A fraction of a molecule cannot exist; some cells must have zero molecules, while others have some or perhaps many molecules. These studies also require killing the cell population and, as such, cannot observe the progression of regulatory events over time. Therefore, we are developing a novel experimental approach based on sequence-specific RNA binding proteins fused to fluorescent reporters, which will allow us to count individual mRNA molecules in single living yeast cells in real time. We are developing two independent such systems, with different RNA sequence specificities and different colors, to simultaneously study the expression of both genes of a divergent pair. By altering the shared promoter site of a divergent pair and literally visualizing the resultant change in transcription, we will tease apart the details of the mechanisms that allow regulatory proteins to regulate only the genes they need to.

In superfluid 3He, silica aerogel acts as an impurity, allowing an otherwise pure system to better model real, impure systems, such as superconductors. However, silica aerogel growth methods vary widely, and, consequently, could be a cause of inconsistencies in recent experiments. Therefore, the ability to structurally characterize silica aerogels is essential to understanding experimental results. The previous characterization method used, x-ray scattering, is a time-consuming and difficult process. We have developed an efficient and economical method to characterize aerogels – optical birefringence. Optical birefringence is a property of anisotropic materials which cause an incident wave to produce two refracted waves. Nucleosome Positioning in Plasmodium Falciparum
The DNA in a eukaryotic cell is orders of magnitude longer than the cell itself. In order to fit inside cells, protein complexes called nucleosomes tightly wrap the DNA. Previous work has shown that nucleosomes prefer to wrap sequences with specific properties. Plasmodium Falciparum-- the organism that causes the most severe form of malaria--has a genome consisting of nearly 80% adenine and thymine, making it highly skewed towards A and T. Sequencing P. falciparum nucleosomal fragments across the genome will allow us to determine whether the sequence preferences predicted by current models are generalizable to AT-rich DNA. I have isolated nucleosomal fragments from P. falciparum and have begun preparing them for sequencing using the ABI-SOLiD system. I have also begun isolating nucleosomal DNA from synchronized P. falciparum cultures at specific stages in its life cycle. Mapping nucleosome positions in several stages of the P. falciparum life cycle allows us to examine regions of DNA upstream of genes specific to one stage and to identify sequences covered by nucleosomes when the gene is not expressed but free of nucleosomes when it is expressed. Regions upstream of differentially-expressed genes occupied by nucleosomes in one stage but not others are likely to contain regulatory sequences. The P. falciparum genome has low information content due to its skewed composition, making it difficult to identify unique regulatory sequences. Mapping nucleosomes across the P. falciparum life cycle and correlating nucleosome occupancy with gene expression could lead to the discovery of novel P. falciparum regulatory sequences.

DNA folds tightly around protein complexes called nucleosomes in order to fit inside our cells. DNA must bend sharply to coil around a nucleosome, and some sequences are more flexible than others. This means that nucleosomes prefer to wrap certain sequences. Previous work demonstrates that the yeast genome uses these preferences to encode favored locations for its nucleosomes. Although the “nucleosome positioning code” successfully explains much of the organization of nucleosomes in yeast, nucleosome positioning in higher eukaryotes is less precisely understood for many reasons. One reason is that mammalian genomes contain very large regions of A+T-rich DNA, and A+T-rich sequences are preferentially excluded from nucleosomes in yeast. This means that the sequence motifs that enable A+T rich sequences to wrap into nucleosomes are unknown. Plasmodium falciparum, the causative agent of malaria, has a highly A+T rich genome. Studying nucleosome organization in the P. falciparum genome will allow nucleosome positioning preferences in A+T rich DNA to be determined. This is an important step to be taken before nucleosomal organization is understood in higher eukaryotes. I have obtained ~10 million nucleosomal sequences from P. falciparum. Analysis of these sequences indicates that like yeast, much of the organization of nucleosomes is encoded by the genome. However, P. falciparum nucleosomal sequences appear to lack the characteristic sequence preferences that define nucleosome positions in all other eukaryotes studied. This suggests that there are novel nucleosome sequence preferences in A+T rich DNA, and I am now working to delineate these undiscovered motifs.

Simulation of Pore Stability in Phospholipid Bilayers
Self-assembled vesicles consisting of a spherical bilayer of lipids surrounding an aqueous core are known as liposomes. Liposomes have emerged as a promising delivery system for potent chemotherapeutic agents. Modified liposomes on the nanoscale have been shown to have excellent pharmacokinetic profiles for the delivery of nucleic acids, proteins, and chemotherapeutic agents. It is important that the liposome system remain stable until it has reached the desired target site at which point it undergoes triggered release due to changes in pH or temperature. Most temperature sensitive liposomes take advantage of the peak in permeability of the bilayer that coincides with a phase transition. At the phase transition temperature, gel and liquid phases coexist and incompatibilities in molecular packing may assist drug release. Unfortunately, many standard liposome compositions result in liposomes that release drugs slowly at the phase transition temperature, and the use of such systems for drug delivery has been unsuccessful. One method to improve the efficiency is to incorporated lysolipids, which are single chain analogues of standard lipids, into liposomes. Lysolipids tend to form micellar structures in aqueous solution. When incorporated in small amounts into lipid systems, it is postulated that lysolipids help to form stable, long lasting pores in the lipid bilayer as it undergoes phase transition from gel to liquid crystalline. However, the characterization of liposome cargo release is a difficult process to probe experimentally. Hence, computational molecular dynamics could be employed to reduce the experimental complications. The Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics model, which helps simplifying the complicated systems, requires less time to simulate and is efficient enough to help understanding the nature of the pore stability in phospholipid bilayers.

Determination of the Envelope-Structure Parameter from Detailed Stellar Models
Binary star systems can be divided into two evolutionary categories: those with non-interacting members and those where interaction occurs. The latter case can present complicated behavior not seen in the evolution of individual stars. One example of interest is the development of a common envelope. This occurs when one of the two stars, called the primary, outgrows its Roche lobe, resulting in gas flowing from the primary to the secondary star. Under certain conditions this can result in a common envelope of gas around the entire system. Predicting what happens next is difficult. It is generally thought that the two stellar cores spiral inward, releasing orbital energy through friction to the envelope. This process then continues until the envelope is expelled. Assuming this model, the final orbital separation of the stellar pair can be obtained from the value of the binding energy of the envelope. This value requires detailed stellar structure models to calculate, and is usually estimated for large scale studies where these aren’t available. In this investigation, such stellar structure models are generated for a wide range of possible stars, and the binding energy is calculated for each. Then a best fit equation is introduced taking basic stellar parameters such as mass, age, and composition, as input, with the binding energy as the dependent variable. The results are to be published for use in large scale studies of contact binaries, greatly increasing precision beyond the currently relied upon estimations.

The common-envelope (CE) phase is an important stage in the evolution of binary stellar populations. The most common way to compute the change in orbital period during a CE is to relate the binding energy of the envelope of the Roche-lobe filling giant to the change in orbital energy. Especially in population-synthesis codes, where the evolution of millions of stars must be computed and detailed evolutionary models are too expensive computationally, simple approximations are made for the envelope binding energy. In this study, we present accurate analytic prescriptions based on detailed stellar-evolution models that provide the envelope binding energy for giants with metallicities between Z=.0001 and Z=0.03 and masses between 0.8 and 100 solar masses, as a function of the metallicity, mass, radius, and evolutionary phase of the star. Our results are also presented in the form of electronic data tables and Fortran routines that use them. We find that the accuracy of our fits is better than 15% for 90% of our model data points in all cases, and better than 10% for 90% of our data points in all cases except the asymptotic giant branches for three of the six metallicities we consider. For very massive stars (M50 solar masses), when stars lose more than ~20% of their initial mass due to stellar winds, our fits do not describe the models as accurately. Our results are more widely applicable (covering wider ranges of metallicity and mass) and are of higher accuracy than those of previous studies.

Exploring Mechanical Networks for the Design of New Materials
When a system is exposed to slowly changing external forces, we can often approximate its reaction by assuming that it remains near equilibrium throughout its evolution. These so-called quasistatic assumptions, which greatly simplify calculations, often result in very accurate models. However, under some conditions, quasistatic assumptions can fail entirely, and a system can undergo sudden changes, even when exposed to slowly changing conditions. Such destabilizations are often associated with a structural failures and undesired behavior. We explore the use of destabilizations to design systems with unexpected and novel behavior. We consider a solid material composed of a network of interacting particles on which an external normal force is exerted. When this force changes, we expect a deformation to result in the direction of the change in applied force. We have shown that, whenever quasistatic approximations are valid, this intuition holds. However, we have also successfully designed a network which undergoes a destabilization due to a change in the applied force such that when the system regains equilibrium, the deformation of the network from its initial configuration is opposite the direction of the change in force. This response is novel and has not been characterized before. From a materials perspective, this destabilization is manifested as a solid-to-solid, stress induced phase transition. A potential application is the construction of new materials which expand under compression or contract under tension.

Documenting a Transnational Pathway: Oaxaca, Mexico to New York, USA
Previous literature on transnational migration has studied migrants moving to urban centers in the United States. This study looks at a population we’ve missed: those who travel to rural receiving regions. The major forces that previous researchers have argued maintain transnational contact are political, religious and social organizations that are all but nonexistent for the migrants arriving in rural regions. This study explores the nuances of transnational life when it is anchored in rural areas of both the sending and receiving countries. Findings are based on a qualitative study of five immigrant families living in rural Western New York and their relatives in San Juan Mixtepec, a small indigenous community in Oaxaca, Mexico. The nature of rural life means people are isolated. No hometown organization helps Mixtepec migrants maintain contact with each other or anyone back home, and Oaxacan politicians do not worry about reaching out to a Western New York contingent of citizens. Furthermore, there are few options for religious involvement in Spanish and no opportunities to worship in Mixteco. Yet these immigrants still live transnational lives, maintaining ties to their home and culture through personal agency, not institutional support. Findings in this study fill a hole in our knowledge of transnational migration by focusing on rural to rural migrants. A revision of theory is necessary with a focus on non-institutional maintenance of transnational ties to fully understand the lived experience of these migrants, a population that comprises almost the entirety of the foreign farmworker population.

Higher reading skill presumes a greater ability to quickly recognize letter strings as words; thus, with reference toward the alternate "missing letter" phenomenon, more skilled readers are expected to show a weaker WSE. An Evaluation of Casuistry as an Effective Way to Approach Applied Ethics
There has been much debate among moral philosophers and practitioners about what method of moral reasoning should be used to best address the issues that arise in applied ethics. Moral reasoning can be understood as the process by which one is able to determine the most morally justifiable action in a particular situation. Therefore, understanding and evaluating this process is very relevant to applied ethics, the study of moral questions within a specific context. Casuistry is a method of moral reasoning that has been a topic of interest in bioethics. It is referred to as having a "case-based" approach to moral reasoning in that moral judgments are arrived at through the use of analogical reasoning with "paradigm cases". Casuistry has been contrasted with the model of principlism (and more recently, specified principlism), which is considered a "principle-based" approach since moral judgments are arrived at deductively through normative principles. I assess the effectiveness of these models, focusing on two criteria: justification and practicality. I argue that none of these models adequately addresses both of these criteria and therefore cannot be considered a unitary account of moral reasoning. I find that justification and practicality often conflict within these models, and some models attempt to strike a balance between the two. I argue that such a balance is not of much use in some areas of practice, and so I propose the conjunction of multiple models with different models being selected depending upon the justificatory or practical requirements of a particular situation.

Attraction Effect in the Domain of Moral Action
Past research has demonstrated that humans tend to rely on emotions and intuitions to drive moral judgments. Furthermore, some researchers have concluded that certain moral intuitions are universal and innate. It is believed that these emotional and intuitive responses generally involve rapid, automatic, and unconscious cognitive appraisals. Proponents of this intuitionist approach say that moral intuitions come first and directly cause moral judgments, and that moral reasoning is usually an ex post facto process. The current study sought to demonstrate that reasoning is not simply a retroactive process, but that it plays an important role in moral judgment. One hundred twenty-eight participants were assigned to one of three conditions, each group receiving a unique moral dilemma. Participants were asked to provide either a positive or negative rating of potential outcomes. We were able to demonstrate strong context effects, shifting average approval ratings of an action by simply adding an additional alternative to initial choice dyads. These findings are important because if universal and innate moral intuitions are the primary drive behind moral judgments, we should have failed to demonstrate context effects. The findings support the initial hypothesis that reasoning is not an entirely retroactive process, and that it plays a significant role in moral judgment.

Jean-Luc Godard and the Modern Cinema of the Parisian Metro
In a 1960s France that was hurtling full speed ahead on the track towards modernity, New Wave filmmaker Jean-Luc Godard realized his first works, attempting to capture the constant movement and unpredictability that characterized the decade. For instance, he would interrupt his main intrigues by inserting documentary-like shots of the streets and crowds of Paris; film anonymous extras in close-up, rivaling the main protagonists’ presence; and drown out dialogue by either overwhelming it through city noises or by cutting sound off all together to create an all-encompassing silence. Consequently, his films not only demonstrated a distinct rupture from the rules that governed classical, narrative cinema, but they also attempted to link together what would appear to be disparate elements and opposing forces. Despite modernity’s overwhelming tendency towards individualism and solitude, Godard yearned to seize the fluid potential at the heart of the metropolitan experience: the notion that we could all possibly be tied to one another; that any seemingly minute encounter could eventually affect society and history; and that we could never have One without taking into consideration the Other. After all, there can be no construction without deconstruction; mobility without immobility; and, above all, no film without a spectator. Cinema, then, if exercised to its fullest potential, could very well break through not only social barriers that normally separate individuals from one another, but also break through its very own barriers, reaching past the screen to directly affect—and possibly even communicate with—its spectator.

The blame for this decline is often placed on the perceived “secularization” of the American university; many commentators on modern religion seem to believe that faith is no longer important or relevant to college students. Although these simultaneous trends seem incongruous and invite further investigation, an analysis of the issues behind this shift in campus religious ecology is absent in current literature about college students and religion. During the 1960s and 1970s, the second wave feminist movement fought for sexual liberation and equality of genders in sexual intimacy and expression. How have media portrayals of sexuality, sexual health and relationships changed from the sexual revolution of the 1970s to now? To assess this research topic, I reviewed both feminist magazines and mainstream magazines from 1970 to 2009. I examined all articles in the feminist publications Off Our Backs and Ms. from this four-decade time period, and all articles from Cosmopolitan and Glamour for the years 1970, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1985, 1989, 1990, 1995, 1999, 2000, 2005, and 2009. I coded each article that mentioned sex, sexuality, or sexual acts, as well as articles discussing related topics such as relationships and dating, sexual danger, sexual health, pornography, prostitution, and sex in media – all set within the United States. My results indicate that feminist publications have greatly decreased the number of articles about sex and sexuality, while in mainstream magazines the topic of sex has proliferated. A content analysis shows that sex issues are no longer framed in a considerably feminist light. Additionally, the integration of feminist topics on sex and relationships has not occurred to a large extent in mainstream media, with the exception of several specific topics. The implications of this data include the absence of a critical perspective on sex in periodical sources. This may give women a limited perspective on how to view sex and heterosexual relationships, which could have a negative effect on gender equality in sexual relationships.

Regulation of Cadmium Stress Response by Chemosensory Neurons in C. elegans
Cadmium is a teratogenic, mutagenic, and potentially lethal heavy metal to which humans are regularly exposed. To address cadmium toxicity, cells rely upon a well-established cellular stress response. The stress response is a transcriptional response wherein specific genes are activated in order to combat the deleterious effects of a particular environmental stressor. Although the stress response confers cytoprotection to cells facing cadmium, stress response induction can have inhibitory effects on growth and division of single cells. Since multicellular organisms depend on coordinated cellular activity, one might expect multi-cellular organisms to have developed systemic mechanisms for regulating the cellular stress response. Indeed, there is evidence that in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans), the function of the heat-sensing AFD neurons can modulate induction of the cellular stress response to heat (the heat shock response). C. elegans have an extensive chemosensory network devoted to cadmium sensation. It is therefore possible that chemosensory input might regulate the cellular cadmium stress response, just as thermosensory input regulates the heat shock response. We show that in C. elegans the activity of a chemosensory neuronal network responsible for cadmium sensation modulates cellular heavy metal stress response activation. Mutations in genes affecting these neurons cause the induction of some, but not all, cadmium stress response genes to be altered in mutant animals. More specifically, our data suggests that the chemosensory neuronal network regulates the cadmium-induced activation of genes that are regulated specifically by the master stress response regulator, the transcription factor Heat Shock Factor 1 (HSF1).

This strategy has been used successfully in intracellular Ca2+ fluorescent probes. Once inside the cell, endogenous esterases will hydrolyze the esters and allow Gd-DOPTA to function as designed. Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by recurrent convulsive seizures that affects over 50 million people, 90% of whom live in developing countries. It is one of the oldest documented diseases, increases a person’s risk for premature death by two to three times, and in America alone has an estimated cost of $15.5 billion/yr. An obvious treatment would be to administer GABA to patients; however, GABA itself can’t cross the blood brain barrier, which is a separation of circulating blood and cerebrospinal fluid that restricts the diffusion of large or hydrophilic molecules into the bloodstream. An alternate and more efficient strategy is to design a GABA-like molecule which can cross the blood-brain barrier and inhibit GABA aminotransferase, an enzyme responsible for the degradation of GABA. Vigabatrin, a commercial drug, uses this method of action and has demonstrated efficacy as an antiepileptic drug for refractory complex partial seizures and for infantile spasms. Vigabatrin, however has serious side effects such as visual blurring and constriction of visual fields. My research this past year has focused on investigating novel GABA inhibitors that could treat epilepsy without deleterious side effects.

Recent advances in high-throughput screening have greatly increased the demand for producing chemical compounds. In an attempt to meet such a demand, organic chemists have turned to solid-phase organic synthesis (SPOS). SPOS is a robust method for synthesizing molecules with benefits including ease of purification, automation, and high yields. Unfortunately, directly applying solution phase chemistry to SPOS is not straightforward and tedious time-consuming reoptimization of reactions is typically required. Therefore, I aim to create materials that combine SPOS with the favorable attributes of solution-phase chemistry without the need for such tedious reoptimization. This approach will be general and thus applicable to the preparation of a diverse range of materials. In order to accomplish this task, I have designed and fabricated a metal-organic framework (MOF) - a hybrid, porous, and crystalline material - that will serve as the scaffold upon which peptides can be synthesized. MOFs have pores that allow diffusion of substrates in and out of the cavities while providing a rigid structure ideal for the post-synthetic modifications required for SPOS. The target MOF was designed to achieve (i) large pore sizes, (ii) easily functionalized sites for the covalent attachment of amino acids, and (iii) favorable stability under the mildly acidic and basic conditions necessary for peptide synthesis. This MOF-based approach could eliminate the current bottleneck in chemical syntheses (i.e. purification) while greatly simplifying the transition from solution phase chemistry to chemistry performed on solid supports. Updating a Classic: A Modern Adaptation of Aristophanes’ Acharnians
My goal in undertaking this project was to make Aristophanes‟ Acharnians, an Ancient Greek comedy, accessible to modern American readers. In this play the protagonist, Dikaiopolis, makes a private peace with Sparta during the Peloponnesian War. Throughout the play, we see how different people have been affected by the war as Dikaiopolis conducts free trade in his private market. First, a Megarian who has been forced into poverty by an Athenian blockade trades his daughters for products which he himself used to export. Later, a servant enters on a young bride‟s behalf, begging Dikaiopolis to share his peace so that the bride‟s husband will not have to fight in the war. Throughout the play, Dikaiopolis also competes with a general, Lamachus, over who has the better life: Dikaiopolis flaunts the luxuries he gains with his peace, while Lamachus boasts about the honors he will win in battle. Agency Attribution and Logic of Action: Intentionality, Morality, and Counterfactual Reasoning
The question of how we judge whether something counts as an action seems at first so basic as to evade analysis. But while psychologists have been largely content to study agency from developmental and perceptual perspectives, philosophers have asked many higher-level questions about what it means to “do” something. In this presentation, I address how the presence of information about counterfactual alternative choices affects decision-making about responsibility for outcomes. To investigate this question, I presented subjects with vignettes about actions and outcomes and asked to decide whether the character in the story “saw to it” that the outcome occur; I varied the probabilities of success given the choice the character made, and some possible choice the character did not make. This evidence does not support two influential views found in the causality literature in psychology (the probabilistic contrast and power PC models). Instead, these data suggest that people use simple heuristic judgments when reasoning about agency; people are sensitive to whether an action made a difference in the likelihood of an outcome, but not to the size of that difference. If people use agentive heuristics, this has substantial implications for philosophy and psychology: For philosophy, because this suggests that we do not derive judgments about actions top-down from a concept of agency; for psychology, because it helps to elucidate how we carve up reality at a basic level, and also opens up the door to investigating cognitive biases for agency, like those discovered by Kahneman and Tversky in other domains.

New Christian Ethics of Forgiveness in Intimate Partner Violence: Exploring Possibilities for Survivor Empowerment
The moral imperative to forgive is at the heart of many influential religious and philosophical traditions, and given the extent of human fallibility, forgiveness is essential in personal relationships. Drawing on the work of several philosophers and theologians like Immanuel Kant and Margaret Farley, my paper examines the norms and limits of forgiveness in personal relationships, where forgiveness is defined as the restoration of intimate relationship. I contend not only that such restoration may not be morally required, but also that certain conditions must be satisfied before it can be considered permissible. Forgiveness, I argue, is ethical only insofar as the relationship it aims to restore is ethical. An ethical relationship is characterized by two norms: mutuality and moral equality. These values are necessary so as to satisfy the requirement of respect for persons in intimate relationships. Furthermore, close examination of these norms reveals that a failure to hold offenders accountable for serious wrongdoing, forgiving them unconditionally, constitutes a failure of respect toward both victims and offenders. Both parties must work together, each taking certain steps, in order to establish a relationship of mutuality and moral equality after wrongdoing. These conditions must be fulfilled if forgiveness is to be a just, life-affirming process rather than a destructive one that perpetuates abuse.

Complementary or Contradictory? Christianity and Platonism in Renaissance Florence
Renewed study of early Platonic philosophers elicited both excitement and condemnation from Italian Renaissance thinkers. While Florentine scholars Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Marsilio Ficino endeavored to demonstrate the compatibility of Neoplatonism and Catholicism, friar Girolamo Savonarola alleged that studying such non-Christian authors would corrupt one's Christian faith. Most research concerning Savonarola treats his denunciations of clerical misconduct and Florentine politics, yet few Renaissance historians have examined the validity of his criticisms of Neoplatonism. This project performs that missing investigation in order to better understand the development of Christianity in a period often viewed as generally secular. The project analyzes two poems on love by the writer Girolamo Benivieni, a friend of Giovnni Pico and Ficino whose early "Song of Love" relies heavily on their ideas. His later devotion to Savonarola led him to renounce the Neoplatonism of his youth and to rewrite the "Song" from a more overtly Catholic perspective. A close reading of the two poems reveals whether Benivieni rejected or reconciled possibly problematic elements of Neoplatonism with early modern Catholicism. My analysis shows that, while Benivieni's Christian work differs markedly from the early poem in its Trinitarian language and standard Catholic cosmology, its omission of the Incarnation and Resurrection of Jesus Christ, grace, and charity indicates possible lingering Neoplatonic influence. While neither poem suggests any growth of the secularism that many view as characteristic of the Renaissance, the study finds that Savonarola's criticisms of Neoplatonism may have been partly true.

Persecution and Expulsion of Loyalists in Maine During the Lead Up to and Early Years of the American Revolution
While at Northwestern University I pursued multiple undergraduate research opportunities in history. During my sophomore year I earned a Leopold Fellowship which gave me the opportunity to work with Professor TH Breen. While reading up on the birth of the American independence movement I became aware of the marginalized colonists who remained loyal to the British Empire, those stories inspired my senior thesis project. During spring break of my sophomore year I traveled to the Nova Scotia Public Archives where I worked with the documents of Jacob Bailey, an Anglican missionary who served in Pownalborough, Maine from 1760 until 1779. Through this research I realized that histories of the American Revolution overlook the profound impact religion had on shaping the conflict by emphasizing the public backlash against Parliament‟s taxation of the colonies as the defining flashpoint between supporters and opponents of Great Britain. Popular preachers drew large crowds, sermons and other religious works were the most widely circulated pamphlets, and churches served as community gathering sites. Because of its major role in daily life, religion became central to delineating political differences. The divide between Congregationalists and Anglicans set boundaries between the two groups over a decade before the tax protests in Boston. In 1774 Bailey penned, “Persecution in politics as well as religion is absurd and will certainly increase the opposition only carried on with unchristian, inhuman and destructive severity.” The quarrel between the two religious groups in Bailey‟s small frontier community originated in 1759 with the Kennebeck Company Proprietors, the town‟s founders, and entered the local government through officials appointed by the proprietors. Bailey‟s letter expresses frustration with the dominance of Congregationalists in Pownalborough‟s government during the years preceding the colonists‟ declaration of independence from Great Britain. In Pownalborough during the Revolution religion coincided with political beliefs; most Congregationalists supported the American Revolution while Anglicans remained loyal to Britain. As a minister in the Church of England Bailey swore an oath to George II who was the head of the Church. That declaration of faith to England put him at odds with the independence movement led by the Congregationalist dominated government. The story of Bailey‟s battle with the Congregationalists demonstrates the broader religious conflict which helped spark the Revolution and, in Maine, divided patriots from loyalists.

A Question of Tolerance: Homosexuality in the Victorian Royal Navy
John Peach was drunk. At least, that was the excuse he and Edward McGee gave when they were found in bed together on the HMS Isis in 1837. Until 1860, the mandatory punishment for sodomy (a catch-all term for sexual contact between men) in the British Navy was death. But neither Peach, nor McGee, nor any sailor charged with a sodomy-related crime was sentenced to death after 1828. Was this a legal fluke, or a sign of potential tolerance? To find out, I traveled to London on a Summer Undergraduate Research Grant to work with the court martial records at the National Archives. Afterwards, I expanded my research into an Independent Study project, and have reached an intriguing conclusion. The average Victorian sailor became relatively indifferent to these commonplace trysts, making the cases unlikely to be reported. In addition, the governing body of the Navy, the Admiralty, hated the bad publicity that came with sodomy trials. So while the Navy officially condemned sodomy, and convicted whomever they could, they preferred sidestepping the issue altogether, including refusing to use terms such as ―sodomy‖ or even ―sex‖ during trials. Sailors who directly addressed the details of their case were therefore more likely to be acquitted by their squirrely judges. Peach and McGee, though caught in a very compromising position, were simply whipped and discharged. This theory suggests that even at this early date, the subject of sex between men generated public outrage coupled with private acceptance.
Fields: History; British History; LGBTQ History

As more and more research demonstrates the health benefits of breastfeeding and the health risks of formula, promoting and supporting breastfeeding has become a key objective of the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC). Currently, women in WIC initiate breastfeeding at a lower rate than the national average and cease to breastfeed before the one year mark recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The goal of this study was to determine what experiences, attitudes, and perceptions influence the infant feeding choices of mothers in different Chicago neighborhoods and how the WIC program could best encourage breastfeeding within the different Chicago clinics. Then, ethnographic interviews were conducted with thirty women at these clinics. The results of my research showed that mothers in Chicago develop an intention to breastfeed through a variety of means: higher education, greater knowledge about breastfeeding, influential people, influential cultural traditions, experiences with healthcare institutions and WIC, and feelings of confidence and commitment. Furthermore, I found that the longer a woman intended to breastfeed, the longer she did in fact breastfeed. However, I also found that women in Chicago encounter many barriers to breastfeeding including physical problems, work and school constraints, lacking time and energy, and social pressures. The most effective way of helping mothers overcome these barriers seemed to be increased education about and help with breastfeeding.

The Mechanisms of Initiation of Symbiosis between Vibrio fischeri SR5 and Euprymna scolopes
The Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes is born sterile, but its light organ is colonized by a single species of bacteria, Vibrio fischeri, within hours of hatching. This symbiotic relationship is essential to the survival of the squid, as the bacterial bioluminescence prevents the squid from casting a shadow while hunting in the moonlit sea, hiding it from predators swimming below. V. fischeri also benefit from the symbiotic relationship, as the squid host provides the bacterial population with nutrients and a competitor-free environment. Although V. fischeri make up less than 0.1% of the bacterial community in the Hawaiian seawater, selective mechanisms exist such that only certain strains of V. fischeri colonize the developing light organ. The V. fischeri/E. scolopes symbiosis is used as a model system to study the mechanisms underlying establishment of symbiosis, as such selective mechanisms are also important in the establishment of human-bacterial symbioses. My research focuses on V. fischeri SR5, a strain that was isolated from the Mediterranean bobtail squid, and is also able to colonize E. scolopes in the laboratory. My work examines the genetic basis of luminescence regulation in V. fischeri SR5 and constitutes the first molecular examination of this strain. I performed a transposon mutagenesis screen for luminescence phenotypes, and isolated 26 strains (out of 9,000 screened) with insertions that significantly altered luminescence. Of these, only strains with an insertion into the gene lrp-encoding the Leucine Responsive Regulatory Protein-also displayed a squid colonization defect. My current research aims to understand the molecular basis for the role of Lrp during the process of squid colonization. I am investigating hypotheses that the colonization defect results from Lrp regulation of bacterial motility and/or its regulation of diffusible signal molecules (autoinducers) utilized in the control of luminescence and colonization pathways.

Testing the Sulfate Initiation Hypothesis for Ocean Anoxic Event 1a
Oceanic anoxic events (OAEs) were short-lived episodes of widespread marine organic carbon burial that occurred during the Cretaceous (145-65 Ma). Characterized by rapid onset, a geologically brief time span, and major perturbations in climate, OAEs represent some of the most profound disruptions of the global carbon cycle preserved in the sedimentary record. Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain these intervals, yet none have satisfactorily accounted for their short-term character and widespread effects. Recent work has focused on the role of sulfur in initiating and terminating OAEs, and more specifically, the potential impact that fluctuating marine sulfate levels may have had on nutrient recycling efficiency, and ultimately, photosynthetic carbon production. To further investigate the potential role that S played in regulating OAEs, we analyzed the C isotope composition of carbonate and the S isotope composition of carbonate-associated sulfate (CAS) and pyrite (FeS2) from sediments collected at Resolution Guyot (ODP Site 866) that straddle the early Aptian OAE1a, one of two major OAEs recognized in the Cretaceous. A decrease of ~5‰ in the S isotope composition of CAS is observed throughout the OAE1a interval, while Δ 34S values (indicative of marine sulfate concentration) remain high and relatively stable during the event. These results, coupled with implications from strontium isotope data, suggest that changes in the S-cycle during OAE1a were dominantly driven by increases in volcanism and hydrothermal activity, and not simply large-scale evaporite deposition that forced a drastic reduction in marine sulfate levels and associated rates of pyrite burial, as previously hypothesized.

Convergence Tests for Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte-Carlo Simulations
With gravitational-wave detection on the horizon, astronomers look for ways of extracting useful information from a detected gravitational wave. Like its electromagnetic cousin, a gravitational wave carries important information about the characteristics of its source, and these characteristics can be recovered through numerical analysis. Using one promising technique known as a Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation, astronomers can produce a probability distribution over an entire parameter space describing gravitational wave signals; given the gravitational wave data, the MCMC produces a sequence of parameter samples whose distribution converges to the probability density on parameter space implied by the data. Although an MCMC simulation will produce the equilibrium probability distribution in an infinite amount of time, a simulation that runs for a finite amount of time may not. This work focuses on using a kD-tree sorting structure to improve MCMC sampling. We show that a simple sampling method effectively recovers an accurate probability distribution in two dimensions but performs worse than a non-interpolated run in nine dimensions. We explain how dimensionality issues and correlations between the nine parameters – which are not taken into account by the simple sampling method – can cause the simple sampling method to yield inaccurate distributions, and we compare these results to those from an interpolated MCMC simulation with a more sophisticated sampling method which takes correlation into account. Improving the convergence of an MCMC simulation through interpolation would allow for faster, more frequent analysis of gravitational wave signals as well as higher confidence in recovered probability distributions.

Identification of a Gene Recruitment Sequence in the GAL1 Promoter
Incorrect gene transcription has been linked to many different human diseases. An understanding of the mechanisms that contribute to gene transcription would assist in understanding and potentially treating these diseases. A gene‘s expression can be affected by its position within the nucleus of a cell. Specifically, a gene‘s location either at the nuclear periphery or in the nucleoplasm may affect its transcription and expression. In the model organism Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer‘s yeast), whose genome bears many similarities to that of humans, some genes are directed to the nuclear periphery via DNA signals called Gene Recruitment Sequences (GRS elements) which are located in gene promoters. The Brickner lab has already identified GRS elements for the yeast genes INO1, TSA2, HSP104, and ACT1. However, the mechanisms controlling the localization of other yeast genes such as GAL1, a well-studied, sugar-responsive gene, are not well understood. My research project seeks to identify the DNA elements responsible for targeting GAL1 to the nuclear periphery in yeast. I have determined that the GAL1 gene has two small, cis-acting GRS elements upstream of its start site in its promoter region. The results of my project will assist in future experiments to identify the proteins involved in GAL1 recruitment and to understand the general molecular mechanism for gene recruitment to the nuclear periphery. My research will also contribute to our understanding of how peripheral targeting affects gene expression.

This process, termed microbial sulfate reduction, reduces sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, which reacts with iron to form pyrite. Pyrite formation removes iron oxides from the ocean, enabling phosphate, a vital nutrient for photosynthesis otherwise removed by sorbtion to iron oxides, to drive primary productivity resulting in widespread anoxia. To test this hypothesis, carbonate associated sulfate (CAS) and pyrite were extracted from sediments spanning OAE2 in France. During the carbon isotope excursion associated with OAE2, CAS is enriched in the heavy isotope of sulfur and pyrite is depleted in the heavy isotope, both of which suggest increased pyrite burial. These data imply that increased marine sulfate levels affected the carbon cycle through the proposed sulfate-phosphate feedback. Furthermore, these results agree with sulfur isotope data from the Western Interior Seaway, suggesting that the oceans were well mixed with respect to sulfate during OAE2.

The Development of Acid-sensitive Peptide Amphiphiles for Enhanced Delivery of Chemotherapeutics
To combat poor targeting and general toxicity of chemotherapeutics, drug delivery systems need to be developed to specifically target tumor cells while leaving noncancerous cells unharmed. We report here a pH-sensitive drug delivery system that targets the acidic microenvironment of tumors using C16H6PEG4 self-assembling peptide amphiphile (PA) nanofibers. The PA nanofibers assemble at physiological pH 7.4 and disassemble below pH 6.5, as characterized by cryogenic transmission electron microscopy, small angle x-ray scattering, and circular dichroism spectroscopy. The chemotherapy drug camptothecin was encapsulated into the PA nanofibers and was tested for selective release in acidic environments. The PA-camptothecin system showed significantly enhanced release by approximately 15% in acidic pH versus physiological pH as measured by dialysis release studies. The PA alone was tested for toxicity against MDA-MB 231 breast cancer cells. The PA showed some toxicity to cancer cells, with reported toxicity of up to 50% in acidic pH and 25% at physiological pH. This is likely due to the increased charge of the PA in acidic pH caused by the protonated histidine residues. The PA-camptothecin system described here is thus a dual-therapy system where both the material toxicity and the drug release rate are enhanced in below-physiological pH. This system shows potential to allow for specific targeting of the acidic tumor microenvironment, while leaving noncancerous cells unharmed.

Economic Development in Long-term Refugee Camps in Ethiopia: A Comparative Study between Eritrean and Somali Refugee Camps
This project strives to contribute to our understanding of the challenges of sustainable economic development in long-term refugee camps by applying behavioral economic theory to livelihoods programs. Data was collected from interviews and surveys conducted by the researcher in Sherkole refugee camp in Ethiopia. UNHCR has promoted livelihoods strategies in protracted refugee situations since the 1970s; however, there are very few successful cases of individuals achieving long-term self-sufficiency in camps. Aid providers promote sustainable self-reliance as a solution to complex protection problems and conceptualize refugees as individual rational actors and industrious entrepreneurs. Narratives collected from long-term refugees in Sherkole Camp refute this image of the refugee. Refugees engage in seemingly impoverishing behavior by volunteering for unpaid leadership positions, sharing limited resources, offering handouts to neighbors, and providing nonproducing loans to one another. Their behavior conflicts with expected utility theory and rational choice, upon which development aid providers base their programmatic designs. As demonstrated in the case study, business failure and greater reliance on rations ensued after the removal of implementing partner resources, disproving NGOs’ claims of sustainable economic development. There is a resultant conflict between self-reliance policy and the on-the-ground realities of refugees’ communal survival strategies and perceptions of their own roles in the camp community. Thus, this paper aims to expound on criticism of livelihoods strategies by examining the role of social capital and applying behavioral economics—including prospect theory, future discount rates, institutions, and trust and reciprocity theory—to provide a more nuanced and accurate economic development framework.

Prodrugs of Inhibitors of the Mevalonate Pathway in Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common pathogenic bacterium and the primary cause of many infections such as pneumonia, meningitis, and many others. This deadly pathogen kills over one million people per year, mostly in developing countries. In the United States, vaccination programs have been used to control this pathogen. Over time, the pathogen has mutated, however, and strains have been found that are resistant to the streptococcus vaccines. Even vancomycin, the antibiotic that is used as a "last resort" to treat these infections, has been showing weaknesses against these new strains of S. pneumoniae. Therefore, a new approach needs to be found to combat this deadly organism. The pathogen requires isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) to survive in human lung or serum. IPP is produced via the mevalonate pathway in three ATP-dependent steps, catalyzed by GHMP family kinases, and is an important building block for isoprenoids. Fluorinated analogs of diphosphomevalonate (DPM) bind to an allosteric site on mevalonate kinase to inhibit the first step in the pathway, while simultaneously mechanistically inactivating the final decarboxylation step of the pathway. This double inhibition is selective for the mevalonate pathway in S. pneumoniae and makes the target compound a potential potent antibiotic against this deadly pathogen. Due to its charged nature, however, diphosphomevalonate is unable to penetrate the cell wall of the bacterium. The purpose of this study, therefore, is to synthesize a series of prodrugs of fluorinated DPM that could potentially penetrate the cell wall, become the desired compound within the cell, and inhibit the mevalonate pathway.
Fields: Medicinal Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Microbiology
Concepts: Streptococcus pneumoniae; mevalonate pathway; mevalonate kinase; diphosphomevalonate; isopentenyl diphosphate; isoprenoid biosynthesis; prodrugs; fluorinated analogs; antibiotic resistance; GHMP kinases; enzyme inhibitors; pneumonia

The Domains of Collagen XV: Elucidating their Role in Pancreatic Cancer
Pancreatic cancer remains one of the deadliest cancers due to its rapid metastasis, lack of early detection methods, and few effective treatment options. Thus, there is an urgent need for more research studying the mechanisms of pancreatic cancer development. Collagen XV, a non-fibrillar collagen located in the basement membrane zone of many tissues, is lost prior to basement membrane invasion in various cancers and acts as a dose-dependent tumor suppressor in vivo. Recently, collagen XV was found to be lost in pancreatic cancer tumors, and in the pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line, BxPC-3, was discovered to inhibit collagen I-induced epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), a program that confers invasive and motile capacities to the cancer cell. My research investigated the role of collagen XV in the suppression of pancreatic tumor progression by studying its interacting partners and the effects of its overexpression on collagen-I induced EMT in the S2-013 pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line. Co-immunoprecipitations revealed collagen XV interacting with DDR1 and E-cadherin, two cell surface receptors aberrantly expressed in many cancers and found to interact with collagen XV in the BxPC-3 cell line. The phosphorylation levels of FAK and PYK2, two downstream kinases of the collagen I pathway, were discovered not to change significantly in collagen XV-expressing cells plated on collagen I although these levels were found to increase and decrease respectively in BxPC-3. Through its interactions with cell surface receptors implicated in various cancers, collagen XV promises to be an important protein in the understanding of pancreatic cancer.
