Group Singing as Treatment for Children's Wellness
Out of the Covid-19 pandemic emerged a mental health crisis, resulting from the prolonged periods of isolation and online interaction. This crisis was especially prevalent amongst children and adolescents, as younger people reported higher levels of depression and anxiety. In response to this crisis, Dr. Sarah Bartolome created the Music for Childhood Well-being Initiative (MCWI), an initiative exploring the impact of singing in a group on children's mental health and wellbeing. In this initiative, 8-week long sessions were conducted where a group of children aged 8-12 were led by an instructor to sing and engage in breathing and stretching exercises. As an Emerging Scholar research assistant, my involvement in this initiative included setting up surveys for the participants to complete, helping participants put on the heart-rate monitoring device we used to collect their heart rate and heart rate variability data, accompanying the singing by playing the piano during sessions, and administering closing interviews for each session. As the sessions progressed, I observed how these sessions led the participants to bond over a sense of community. This became something that all the participants looked forward to every week, and even if participants admitted to entering the room feeling tired, they usually left feeling happy after the session's activities. Further implications of this research could involve the exploration of utilizing group singing as a potential mental health treatment for demographics beyond children, as it has proved to be effective amongst children in MCWI sessions.

Living, Working, and Playing: Asian American Environmental Justice Before the Movement
In 1991, over one thousand environmental activists of color gathered in Washington, D.C. for the First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit, marking the beginning of the environmental justice (EJ) movement. To formally define EJ, they ratified the seventeen Principles of Environmental Justice, highlighting the unequal environmental burdens that low-income communities of color face and redefining the environment itself to include not only the natural wilderness, but also spaces where humans live, work, and play. Despite the movement's increased inclusivity and reach since 1991, scholars and the general public have overlooked Asian American EJ activism because of the pervasive model minority myth, which casts Asians as deferential, apolitical machines alienated from nature. To counter this misconception, my paper examines three cases of Asian American organizing that contain EJ characteristics but lack scholarly analysis of this dimension because they occurred prior to the movement. Using the seventeen Principles, I analyze San Francisco Chinatown's bubonic plague outbreak in 1900, Hawai'i's sugar strike in 1946, and San Francisco Manilatown's International Hotel movement in the 1970s. I argue that, throughout their long history of organizing around issues like civil rights, labor rights, and housing, Asian Americans were fighting for environmental justice long before the movement began. My paper demonstrates it is possible to apply the modern EJ framework to pre-movement history, and I encourage historians to reexamine their areas of study accordingly. Ultimately, I aim to dispel stereotypes about Asian American apoliticalness and uncover a hidden thread of Asian American history.

Isolating the Utility of Planning Against a Dynamic Threat in Naturalistic DecisionMaking
Traditionally, research on choice-based behavior has relied on simple, static experimental setups that lack ecological validity. To address this limitation, the Dombeck Lab and MacIver Lab have developed a large arena with reconfigurable obstacles and an autonomous robotic predator, allowing for the systematic manipulation of environmental structure and threat dynamics. Using high-resolution tracking of a mouse's position and velocity, this system enables detailed characterization of navigational strategies, escape behaviors, and decision-making processes during predator evasion and reward-seeking. Previous work using this arena demonstrated that increasing environmental complexity through the addition of obstacles enhances the utility of planning; while in open, obstacle-free environments, mice tend to rely on habitual, stereotyped routes that minimize deliberation. In the present study, we ask whether planning-like behavior can emerge even in a low-complexity, open arena when a dynamic and behaviorally relevant element is introduced. Specifically, we examine whether the presence of a behaviorally-complex, mobile, interactive threat is sufficient to disrupt habitual navigation and elicit behavioral signatures consistent with planning. By isolating dynamic threat from static spatial complexity, this work aims to clarify the conditions under which planning becomes computationally advantageous in naturalistic decision-making.

Exploring fathers' health behavior motivations to leverage healthcare engagement in the perinatal period: A qualitative study
Commonly, fathers engage in their partner's healthcare in the perinatal (e.g. obstetrics appointments) but underutilize their own healthcare and preventive care services. Thus, researching ways to better engage fathers with healthcare services by leveraging perinatal contact and fathers' perinatal-specific motivations may provide opportunities for health promotion of fathers. Thus, semi-structured interviews with new fathers (n=30) and paired mothers (n=10) in Prentice Women's Hospital were conducted to explore perspectives on and experiences of fathers' health behaviors in the perinatal period. Interview transcripts were cleaned and thematically analyzed based on the Health Belief Model. It was found that fathers were generally highly motivated to maintain or improve their own health in the perinatal period. Being an "active father," longevity for family's sake, and "groundedness" from new fatherhood were important motivations for engaging in positive health behaviors (i.e. exercise, healthy diet, limiting substances use). Low perceived susceptibility to chronic disease and social norms against healthcare engagement were cited as deterrents for preventive healthcare utilization. Time constraints, insurance, and difficulty navigating the healthcare system were cited as barriers to actionable healthcare engagement despite increased motivation. Both fathers and mothers mentioned that leveraging family-centered rather than individual motivations while providing ease to healthcare access (e.g. health screenings in OB settings; efficient primary care referrals) could be effective. This study highlights the potential efficacy of the perinatal period as a leveraging period for engaging fathers with healthcare and offers insight into more broadly expanding health programming for fathers.

Effects of Independence and Interdependence Priming on Big Five Personality Trait Reporting
Personality assessments such as the Big Five are often assumed to reflect stable individual traits, yet growing evidence suggests that responses may be shaped by contextual and cultural factors, including how individuals construe themselves in relation to others. This study examined whether priming independence versus interdependence influences personality trait reporting, and whether individual differences in self-construal predict variation in responses. Participants (N = 117) first completed baseline Big Five (BFI-2) and self-construal measures. In a second session, participants were randomly assigned to an independence or interdependence priming task before completing anchoring vignettes designed to reduce reference group bias in personality judgments. The priming manipulation did not produce significant group-level differences in vignette-adjusted personality ratings. As a result, multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine whether individual differences in self-construal predicted trait reporting while controlling for baseline personality. Across all five traits, baseline Big Five scores were strong and consistent predictors of vignette-adjusted ratings (all p & .001). However, neither interdependence nor independence scores significantly predicted trait ratings for any domain (all p > .13). These findings suggest that personality reporting, even when adjusted for reference group bias, is largely stable and not easily influenced by brief contextual primes or individual differences in self-construal. This has implications for theories of cultural variation in personality, highlighting potential limits on the malleability of self-reported traits in experimental contexts.

Fingertip-Sized Wireless Button Sensors for Health Monitoring in Neonatal and Pediatric Patients
The button sensors project aims to develop fingertip-sized devices for wirelessly monitoring vital signs of preterm patients in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Three discrete units-ECG/EEG (chest/head), PPG (head), and mechano-acoustic (peripheral)-work in tandem to provide comprehensive measurements of key vitals: heart rate, respiration, blood oxygen level, EEG, heart rate variability, sleep, motion, and temperature. Each unit includes electronic components encapsulated by medical-grade silicone or epoxy, which protects sensitive neonatal skin from abrasion and ensures longevity of the device. One significant technical achievement of the project was successfully miniaturizing photoplethysmography (PPG) for the head unit, enabling measurement of peripheral oxygen saturation with increased space optimization and power-efficiency. The sensors are supported by two power supply options-wireless power transfer technology or a miniature magnet-connected battery-which can be easily interchanged to reduce data dropouts. Altered Foodways: The Impact of Colonialism on PCOS Prevalence in the Andes
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a reproductive and metabolic disorder caused by both genetic and dietary factors. The prevalence of PCOS within a population is particularly high among the indigenous populations of the global south, compared to rates in European populations. This study examines the prevalence of PCOS among indigenous and mestizo Andean populations and considers the impact of colonialism and changing foodways on the emergence of this condition. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature review compiled academic journal articles on PCOS rates, foodways, and Spanish colonial policy in the indigenous Andes from the 16th century to 20th century. The implementation of a tribute economy and debt peonage system disrupted indigenous agricultural practices and access to domestic foods, resulting in changes in dietary patterns. Additionally, increase in trade from lowlands to highlands resulted in increased availability of non-traditional foodstuffs, creating social pressure to adopt a non-traditional diet for social mobility. Both of these developments resulted in increased reliance on imported and processed foods over traditional, domestic foods that continued into the 20th century. Comparative evidence suggests that shifting from a subsistence diet to one high in simple carbohydrates and fats resulted in body composition and metabolic health that promoted the emergence of PCOS. Understanding the effect of colonialism on contemporary agrarian practices and foodways unveils underlying systems that raise PCOS prevalence within this population, allowing them to be targeted for treatment.

Internal Fact-Checking and the Crisis of Trust in News Mediaa
This thesis examines the role of fact-checking in addressing the crisis of trust in American news media, asking whether current practices meaningfully improve public understanding or credibility. While fact-checking has become a prominent journalistic tool, this project argues that its dominant form-external, post-publication verification of political claims-faces structural limitations that prevent it from achieving its intended audience-facing goals. Drawing on interviews with leading practitioners, including Glenn Kessler of The Washington Post, Kimberly Ammiano of the CBS Evening News research team, and Zach Helfand of The New Yorker, as well as historical and case analysis and research in media psychology, the thesis compares external fact-checking with internal, pre-publication verification processes. It finds a disconnect between the "imagined" effects of external fact-checking, as described by journalists, and its "real" effects on audiences, which are shaped by factors such as selective exposure, motivated reasoning, and declining institutional trust. While fact-checking has at times imposed reputational costs on political actors, evidence suggests it rarely produces lasting changes in public beliefs. The project argues that strengthening internal fact-checking within original reporting-rather than relying primarily on reactive, standalone corrections-offers a more effective way to ensure accuracy reaches audiences at the point of consumption. By reframing fact-checking as a proactive rather than corrective practice, this research offers a potential solution in the consolidation of fact-checking efforts that prioritizes internal fact-checking, and contributes to ongoing debates about journalistic responsibility, media credibility, and the future of truth-seeking in a fragmented information environment.

How Bacteria Tell Time: Mathematical Models of the Cyanobacterial Circadian Clock

In nature, however, this biochemical process is subject to biological noise, including random fluctuations in environmental conditions, rate constants, and protein concentrations. This project develops "noisy" stochastic models of the cyanobacterial clock to test the validity of the ODE framework under biologically relevant noise conditions and to better analyze sensitivities of this biochemical process. The noise tolerance of each parameter was determined by identifying statistical variation between the trajectory of stochastic simulations and the period of the ODE model. Statistical analysis of the stochastic simulations revealed that the model is highly tolerant to random fluctuation in ATP and the concentration of unphosphorylated KaiC, consistent with the fact that these parameters are most susceptible to noise in a natural environment. Analysis also revealed that the model is sensitive to minor fluctuation in the concentrations of KaiA and sequestered KaiC, a new insight gained through stochastic modeling. These results exhibit how stochastic modeling can validate and refine mathematical models of biochemical processes and reveal underlying sensitivities of a biochemical system to drive future experimentation.

Clean Conscience: Exploring College Students' Enactment of Environmental Beliefs Through Domestic Labor

I tested three hypotheses regarding feminized environmental action from the aforementioned literature: the maternal responsibility, knowledge support, and economic salience hypotheses. Probabilistic Neural Operator for Dynamical Systems Under Uncertainty
In everyday life, we encounter many systems that evolve over time, known as dynamical systems. Examples include vibrations in structures, weather patterns, financial markets, and the spread of diseases. Scientists and engineers have studied these systems for many years, but traditional models often struggle to take full advantage of the large amounts of data now available. Such models also rarely tell us how reliable their predictions are. Our research aims to develop a new data-driven modeling approach using neural operators, a modern machine learning technique that learns how entire systems change over time. Unlike standard models, our approach not only predicts future behavior based on past observations but also estimates how confident those predictions are. To achieve this, we incorporate ideas from statistics, such as quantile regression and Bayesian methods, to explicitly account for uncertainty. By doing so, the model can capture both errors in the data (from sensors that record noisy, imperfect measurements) and limitations in the model itself. As a result, our method produces predictions along with confidence intervals, giving users a clearer understanding of possible outcomes and risks. We compare our approach with existing methods that estimate uncertainty. Preliminary results suggest that our approach achieves similar or better predictive performance, while providing more trustworthy confidence intervals with a simpler and more efficient framework. Such reliability is especially important for decision-making in areas like healthcare, climate science, and finance, where uncertainty plays a critical role.

The King and Queen of Rock: Little Richard, Religion, and the Stipulations of Black Queer Fame

Additionally, reflections on personal experiences undergoing triage revealed considerations patients make about leaving the waiting room and in some cases, choosing alternative healthcare provider options. HANDFUL: Dexterous Multi-Step Robot Manipulation with Resource Awareness
Dexterous robot hands offer rich opportunities for multi-step manipulation: for example, grasping an object and then pushing another object, pulling a drawer, or pressing a button. However, most prior work in dexterous manipulation focuses on single, isolated tasks. In contrast, our key insight is that these multi-step manipulation tasks require resource-aware grasps where the robot must conserve fingers for later actions rather than simply optimizing an initial whole-hand grasp in isolation. We introduce HANDFUL, a learning framework that treats finger usage as a limited resource and rewards the robot for exploring one- and two-finger grasps that leave fingers and in-hand space available for downstream tasks. These grasps are then efficiently selected and trained for downstream tasks via curriculum-based policy learning We further propose HANDFUL-Bench, a simulation benchmark that introduces sequential dexterous manipulation tasks across multiple second-subtask objectives, including pushing, pulling, and pressing, under a shared grasp + second objective setup. Second objectives include: pushing another object, pressing a button, twisting a knob, pulling a drawer, and grasping a second object. Results show that resource-aware grasp planning improves both success rate and robustness compared to a baseline that greedily optimizes the initial grasp before attempting the second subtasks. We additionally validate our approach on a real dexterous hand. Together, this work establishes resource-aware grasp planning as a key principle for multi-step dexterous manipulation. Supplementary material is available on our website: [handful-dex.github.io] (http://handful-dex.github.io).

Inafa'maolek Archaeologies: CHamoru heritage resurgence amidst U.S. militarization on Guahan (Guam)
The rise of U.S. militarization on Guam and the passage of federal laws governing cultural resource management and environmental protection have rapidly increased archaeological surveying over the last few decades. This research investigates the role of CHamorus, the Indigenous people of Guam and the Mariana Islands, who work as archaeologists and historic preservationists to steward Indigenous cultural heritage amidst military build-up. These applied anthropologists play a crucial role in protecting CHamoru heritage, working with archaeological materials spanning up to 4,000 years old that connect present day CHamorus to ancient ancestors. Using ethnographic methods, including participant observation and semi-structured interviews, this research examines how CHamoru archaeologists and historic preservationists are incorporating CHamoru knowledge systems throughout their work on their ancestral homelands, focusing on the newly constructed Marine Corps Camp Blaz base. This research maps the current institutional landscape of heritage management on Guam, identifying some of the challenges of CHamoru archaeologists and historic preservationists within their work. For these practitioners, archaeology has been utilized as a site of resistance towards colonial knowledge production on the CHamoru people. Drawing on Indigenous and activist archaeological literature, this research explores how CHamoru practitioners are subsequently navigating Indigenous identity, community, and place-making as they work on specific heritage sites. By centering CHamoru relationships to land and prioritizing community access, CHamoru practitioners in the field are utilizing archaeology as a tool to foster sovereignty through decolonial heritage education, while simultaneously mobilizing to protect Indigenous cultural landscapes amidst violent militarization.

Decoding Cave Wall Patterns to Search for Life Elsewhere
Caves on Mars and the Moon suggest that similar environments on Earth can help scientists search for signs of life beyond our planet. One promising avenue of research is focused on "biovermiculations" - worm-like patterns of microbe-rich material that form on cave walls. Most studies of these features come from sulfur-rich caves, where microbes drive their formation through sulfur-based chemistry. This study examines biovermiculations in Mammoth Cave, Kentucky, a limestone cave with different environmental conditions, to better understand how they form and whether they are truly biological in origin. Our hypothesis is that biovermiculations in non-sulfur caves are shaped by active microbial processes. We combined microscopy, spatial mapping, and DNA analysis techniques to analyze these patterns. In Mammoth Cave, biovermiculations appear across five distinct morphologies and are made from materials like soot, mud, and cricket guano. Their form is influenced more by the type and behavior of available material than by nearby patterns. Microscopy revealed motile microorganisms that could actively rearrange material on cave surfaces. We also found that these features have developed over at least the past century, growing into 19-20th century soot deposits but not significantly affecting newer ones (post-1970). Genetic analyses show that the microbial communities within biovermiculations are distinct from other sites and share similar compositions across samples. Many of these microbes are associated with sulfur and iron cycling, as well as methane use, suggesting diverse metabolic activity. These findings help refine how scientists identify signs of life in cave-like environments on other planets.

My Tutor Bot: Integrating Large Language Models into Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Fundamental Programming
This research explores how integrating large language models (LLMs) into intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) can enhance student learning outcomes in fundamental programming courses. Building on findings that combining computer-based and human tutoring is highly effective, this study examines how LLMs can replicate the benefits of human tutors, such as personalized feedback and scaffolding, while offering scalable, adaptive support. To investigate this, I implemented "My Tutor Bot" within Northwestern's Comp Sci 211 across Winter and Spring Quarters 2026, creating a trustworthy, instructor-controlled environment by training the LLM exclusively on Professor Zhang and Hummel's course materials. If a student has any questions beyond the scope of the provided course materials, My Tutor Bot informs them that it cannot respond. My Tutor Bot is also FERPA-compliant and built to protect students' privacy. This ensures a safe space for students to explore content and receive 24/7 adaptive scaffolding tailored to the curriculum. By analyzing chat logs, interviews, and surveys, the research evaluates the impact of targeted AI tutoring on conceptual understanding, student engagement, and educational equity. The results aim to identify best practices for leveraging AI in academic settings and provide insights into how LLM-driven ITS can close equity gaps and improve learning outcomes in STEM fields.

Auditory Processing and Behavioral Responses to Sound During Sleep
Sleep has traditionally been viewed as a state of sensory disconnection, but past studies have found that the brain continues to process external stimuli across sleep stages, with sensory responses maintained during REM sleep. Prior research also found that behavioral responses to auditory lexical-decision tasks can occur during sleep, but most participants do not recall these interactions upon awakening unless they experience lucid dreams. In this study, we investigated when external sounds become incorporated into dreams and whether real-time behavioral responses can occur without conscious awareness. Participants were trained to associate five distinct sounds with specific sniffing patterns. These cues were presented during N2, N3, and REM sleep, followed by awakenings after delays of 0.5, 3, or 10 seconds to collect dream reports and assess recall. Across 78 analyzed awakenings, participants were able to volitionally respond to external stimuli during sleep through sniffing responses. Among these awakenings, 16 total incorporation trials were observed: 5 during N2 sleep, 2 during N3 sleep, and 9 during REM sleep. This suggests that REM may be the most receptive stage for integrating external stimuli into dream content. Overall, these findings show that the sleeping brain can respond to external stimuli in real time. This work has implications for applications in dream research, memory consolidation, and sleep-based interventions.

Infants Can Reason About Objects Even When They Are Hidden: Evidence from Containment Events
Before infants can speak, hearing an object (e.g., my cat) named influences how they represent it-as an individual ("Misty") or a category member (CAT). These distinct representations affect infants' memory: when an object is named with a distinct name, but not a category name, infants encode that object as a unique individual and distinguish it from other objects. Here, we ask whether naming objects also has downstream consequences for infants' reasoning about the objects in dynamic events. In two ongoing experiments, 12- and 16-month-olds (planned N=96) participate via Zoom. All infants are full-term and primarily English-exposed. In Experiment 1, infants first see videos of four plush bunnies that differ only in color, and each bunny is labeled with a distinct novel noun. Then, in the test videos, the last-named bunny (blue bunny) is hidden inside a small container and then retrieved after a pause. In the no-change event, the same-colored bunny is retrieved. In the change event, a different colored bunny (pink bunny) is retrieved. Experiment 2 is identical to Experiment 1, except the four bunnies are first labeled with the same name. We expect infants to look longer at the test event they find unexpected. Preliminary results revealed that infants looked longer at the change than the no-change event in Experiment 1, suggesting that both 12- and 16-month-olds successfully reasoned about the individual bunnies when they had distinct names. This work extends prior work to reveal new insights about infants' early link between language and cognition.

Method Matters: Including Critical Race Theory in the Academic Tradition of Qualitative Meaning Making
Critical Race Theory (CRT) recognizes race as a social construct. It examines and acknowledges how race is embedded in policies, institutions, and social structures. The current social and political climate asserts that racism shouldn’t be interrogated, and the lived experiences of people of color aren’t mediated by race. As a result, Critical Race Theory has been under attack and delegitimized as a credible research framework. However, utilizing CRT as a framework and analytical lens in qualitative research allows for rich and diverse stories to be expressed. Specifically analyzing the case study methodology, which is a detailed examination of an event or phenomenon, this study worked to understand how CRT can be used in case studies and inform the narratives that can be communicated. To investigate, I created research outlines, conducted a literature review, and completed annotated bibliographies on CRT and its application in case studies. I discovered that using CRT in case studies isolates and highlights race to uncover the impacts of race and racism on people of color’s lives, validating people of color's experiences with racism. As racism continues to affect people of color negatively, understanding how race shapes lived experience is essential for driving meaningful policy and structural reform. This research has direct implications for how race-centered studies and research involving people of color are designed and conducted. Further development of CRT within qualitative research methodologies is warranted to deepen meaning-making and expand the range of stories that academic research can share.

Cortical Interneurons in the Mouse Model of Fragile X
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects how people communicate, learn, and interact with the world, and it impacts more than 1% of people globally. One of the most common inherited causes of ASD is Fragile X syndrome, which occurs when the FMR1 gene is turned off. Researchers believe that many ASD symptoms may result from an imbalance between excitatory brain signals, which increase activity, and inhibitory signals, which calm activity down. In Fragile X syndrome, this imbalance may be caused by the loss or reduced function of inhibitory brain cells called interneurons. This project investigates whether the death or dysfunction of these interneurons in early development contributes to this imbalance. Using a mouse model of Fragile X syndrome, we focus on the somatosensory cortex, the part of the brain that processes sensory information such as touch. Specifically, we study parvalbumin- and somatostatin-containing interneurons, which help regulate brain activity and are critical for normal circuit development. To track these cells, we use genetically modified mice in which interneurons luminesce red under fluorescent microscopy. Brain tissue is collected at key stages of early postnatal development, sectioned, and imaged to count interneurons and inhibitory synapses across different layers of the cortex. Additional staining methods allow us to measure markers of inhibitory connections. By comparing Fragile X mice to healthy controls, we aim to determine whether reduced interneuron survival helps explain cortical hyperexcitability in ASD. Identifying when and where these changes occur could guide future therapies designed to restore healthy brain circuit balance in autism.

Developing a cFos Atlas to map brain activity
Light plays a critical role in regulating physiological and behavioral processes, yet the neural circuits underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) contribute to functions such as circadian photoentrainment, mood regulation, and thermoregulation, and project broadly throughout the brain, mapping their downstream signaling pathways is essential for understanding how light impacts brain function. This project aimed to investigate how ipRGCs influence brain-wide activity by developing a c-Fos-based activity atlas. C-Fos, an immediate early gene, was used in order to detect the areas of the brain that are activated upon light exposure. To accomplish this, two groups of mice were used: a control group maintained in darkness and an experimental group exposed to a brief light pulse. Following stimulation, brains were extracted, coronally sectioned, and processed using immunohistochemistry to label c-Fos. Additional markers, including NeuN and ChAT, were used to identify neuronal populations. Fluorescent imaging enabled visualization of activity patterns across brain regions. The resulting dataset provides a foundational framework for constructing a whole-brain c-Fos atlas of light-responsive activity, revealing distinct regions activated in response to ipRGC stimulation. This work establishes a reference map that can be used to compare activity patterns in future studies, including models lacking ipRGC function, to better define the role of these cells in neural circuits. Ultimately, this research advances a systems-level understanding of how light influences brain function and behavior, with broader implications for circadian biology and mood-related disorders.

When Silence Speaks: Comparing Conversational Delays in Schizophrenia and Depression
Psychosis is a mental health condition in which an individual exhibits severe impairments in the ability to discern between what is real and what is not. While psychosis is generally known for presenting as hallucinations and delusions, a growing body of literature has also identified speech abnormalities in psychotic patients, characterized by lulls in conversational turn-taking. More specifically, these individuals tend to have extended pauses before answering questions. Our research aims to extend these findings by differentiating delays in response latency between individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) and those at clinical high-risk (CHR) for psychosis. These findings could be used to assess potential differences in symptomatology in order to better distinguish early-warning signs of psychosis from other mood disorders. Through retrospective analysis of clinical interviews, our team has categorized speech patterns to investigate whether response latency differs significantly between MDD and CHR populations. Observed differences in turn-taking delays may be indicative of distinct underlying mechanisms in social functioning and could support conversational turn-taking as a behavioral biomarker for assessing psychotic risk. This could have major implications in improving early detection of psychosis by enabling timely intervention and thereby optimizing long-term clinical outcomes.

PRL2 and the PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling pathways in T-ALL
T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive blood cancer that comprises 10-13% of leukemia diseases in children. Certain signaling pathways, such as the PI3K/PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway in these T-ALL cancer cells are switched on and promote the progression of the disease. Many of these pathways are controlled by oncogenes such as PRL2 (Phosphatase of Regenerating Liver 2), which are proteins that promote unregulated cell division and growth that are characteristic of cancer cells. This project aims to determine if PRL2 promotes cancer growth by disabling the PTEN tumor suppressor and therefore activating the PI3K/PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. To investigate this signaling pathway, we sequenced for different conditional mouse models to observe the interactions of these proteins: PRL2 -/- (KO), PTEN WT; PRL2 -/- (KO), PTEN +/- (F/+); PRL2 +/+ (WT), PTEN WT; PRL2 +/+ (WT), PTEN +/- (F/+). By isolating and analyzing the DNA sequences offetal mouse livers, we created four different groups of mice DNA with different genetic combinations, including mice that lacked the PRL2 protein (knockout mice, KO). Creating these conditional groups of mice allows us to isolate the mechanisms of PRL2 and how it influences the spread and severity of disease. Knockout of PRL2 allows us to determine if PTEN regains function and reduces overall disease progression in mice and the mechanisms behind it. We hope our findings will help us determine a new way to prevent cancer growth through targeted therapies, leading to better survival rates and treatments for pediatric T-ALL cases.

How Crm1 Brings Genes to the Nuclear Edge-and the Proteins That Help It
Cells regulate gene activity not only through molecular signals but also by physically organizing DNA within the nucleus. Recent research suggests that genes positioned near structures called nuclear pores can become more active. A protein called Crm1, best known for transporting molecules out of the nucleus, also helps bring genes to these locations, acting as a docking factor that influences gene activity. However, the additional factors required for this process remain unknown. Crm1 is also frequently overactive in human cancers, but the mechanisms underlying its role in disease are not fully understood. This project aims to identify proteins that cooperate with Crm1 in controlling gene positioning and activity. Using a yeast model system, mutations are introduced throughout the genome and compared between normal cells and cells with elevated levels of Crm1. Mutations that reduce the harmful effects of excess Crm1 are analyzed to identify candidate proteins involved in this pathway. This work aims to uncover the network of factors that enable Crm1 to position genes at the nuclear periphery, providing new insight into how spatial organization influences gene expression. Understanding this mechanism may help explain how disruptions in nuclear organization contribute to diseases such as cancer.

Black Players, White Schools: How integration reshaped Southern college football
The landscape of college football has long been shaped by unequal access to power, resources, and visibility, yet one sector of programs remains consistently overlooked: historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs). This paper challenges the common narrative of integration as a straightforward success story by revealing how it reproduced new forms of inequality within the sport. Understanding this dynamic not only reframes the history and temporality of college football but also helps explain the persistent disparities in funding, exposure, and institutional power that continue to shape the game today. In my research, I argue that the integration of college football in the 1960s and 1970s, particularly in the South, did not benefit the Black community; it actually harmed it. Integration reshaped the sport in ways that pulled talent, money, and attention away from historically Black colleges and universities and concentrated them towards predominantly white institutions (PWIs). Drawing on a combination of academic sports scholarship and primary sources, including Black newspapers and collegiate publications, my research uses a chronological and comparative analysis to trace how integration unfolded across regions and institutions. By examining key case studies, including the rise of HBCU programs, the structure of segregated PWI football, and pivotal moments such as the integration of major Southern powerhouses, the paper shows how success by integrated teams prompted PWIs to recruit Black athletes for competitive advantage rather than moral progress. This shift concentrated visibility and resources within already dominant programs, weakening the institutional and cultural centrality of HBCU football.

Novel Strategies for Assessing Awareness in the Borderlands between Sleep and Wake
Our study aims to exploit lucid dreaming, the state of being aware of dreaming while in a dream, to investigate the threshold between wake and sleep. The goal of the study is for napping participants to provide signals about their experience in response to auditory cues during sleep-onset, the period when the body transitions into sleep. Part of the challenge for participants is to retain memory of their experiences after awakening. Electrodes for monitoring sleep physiology are applied to participants' scalp and face. Prior to a 90-minute nap, participants listened to a 3-beep cue while cultivating mental clarity of being aware of the present moment. These cues were presented again during sleep to reactivate that mental clarity, so that participants could signal about their subjective state. They were instructed to frown to indicate feeling asleep or smile to indicate feeling awake. Participants were awoken periodically to provide a report of their experience and complete a standard set of questions. EEG data were analyzed to determine participants' sleep stage. Data collection is ongoing, and so far 62 trials have been completed on 5 participants. Out of these 62 trials, in 7 (11%), an awake participant reported feeling asleep and in 12 (19%), a sleeping participant reported feeling awake. This provides evidence for the prevalence of sleep-state misperception, in which participants incorrectly perceive whether they are asleep or awake. These results open the door to asking more about why awareness does not always line up with objective sleep state.

Functionalizing Yarns with Dip Coating for Smart Knitted Haptic Tactile Interfaces
The human skin is lined with several mechanoreceptors that are constantly converting things like pressure, vibration and textures into tactile signals that our brain can interpret. Replicating a small portion of this sensitivity into everyday materials would make sensing possible without being intrusive. However, the process is limited by the material as there are no commercially available conductive yarns that are machine knittable, flexible, and insulated in a way that can be useful for research and prototyping. This project addresses this problem by developing a low-cost dip coating process that produces custom insulated conductive yarns compatible with knitting machines. We studied the effects that varying mechanical, chemical, and environmental parameters had on coating uniformity, thickness, and electrical isolation. These knitted items were used to create capacitive sensing pressure arrays that mimic mechanoreceptors and triboelectric nanogenerators for low power embedded systems. Optimization of Carbon Black in Conversion Cathodes: Investigation of Additive Impurities
The growing environmental concerns associated with fossil fuels have driven demand for sustainable energy alternatives, the adoption of electric vehicles, and the decarbonization of the electric grid. In order to support this transition, there is an increasing need for more energy-dense lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) to support electrification. A typical battery consists of three main components: the anode, cathode, and electrolyte, with the cathode composed of an cathode active material, conductive additive, and binder. While conventional cathodes rely on cobalt- or nickel-based intercalation materials, these face supply risks and are nearing their theoretical capacity limits. Conversion cathodes are a promising alternative which offers 200-300% higher energy density than traditional intercalation cathodes. Here, we study FeF2 conversion cathodes, which have been extensively studied due to their high energy density, low cost, and mineral abundance. However, due to low electronic conductivity, conversion cathodes require ~30% conductive additive, whereas intercalation cathodes typically achieve ~90% active mass loading. To overcome this, my research involved optimizing carbon black conductive additives by investigating their composition, electrochemical performance, and impurities. Commercial and impurity-rich carbon blacks were analyzed using galvanostatic cycling and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) to investigate the effect of impurity concentration on cycling performance. It was demonstrated that Li-ion half-cells fabricated using sulfur-rich carbon black samples suffered a loss of long-term cycle stability. These results suggest that controlling impurity chemistry in conductive additives is crucial for the overall performance of Li-ion batteries.

Say what again? Investigating the intelligibility of Formula 1 driver speech between situations, contexts, and language backgrounds
This study investigated how background noise and speaker characteristics affect intelligibility in real-world contexts, specifically by using naturally occurring speech samples from Formula 1 drivers in different race-related situations. Thus, this study extends controlled laboratory-based research on speech-in-noise recognition to a naturally occurring, high-stakes communicative situation. We compiled a corpus of 630 utterances from 21 Formula 1 drivers (9 first-language English speakers, 12 second-language English speakers) across three acoustic environments: studio interviews (minimal noise), paddock interviews (moderate noise), and race communications (high noise). Utterances from 4 first-language English speakers and 4 second-language English speakers then were selected to form the experimental stimulus set. 51 first-language English-speaking listeners (ages 22–81) transcribed 96 experimental utterances (8 speakers × 3 noise conditions × 4 utterances) in a web-based task. Participants were randomly assigned to either see contextual question prompts while listening to each utterance or transcribe utterances without contextual support. Transcriptions were scored using Autoscore, an automated scoring software (Borrie et al., 2019). Results revealed substantial effects of background noise, speaker native language status, and contextual support on intelligibility. Intelligibility increased progressively from race to paddock to studio conditions. Participants correctly transcribed utterances from first-language English speakers at a higher rate than second-language English speakers. Contextual prompts improved intelligibility, with benefits increasing as noise levels increased. These findings reveal the compounded communication challenges in Formula 1 and, by extension, other real-world speech communication situations where speakers must communicate in their second language while contending with extreme acoustic degradation during high-pressure situations.

AI-Assisted Validation of Transfer Data in Economic Research
Largescale economic research increasingly relies on structured datasets compiled from hundreds of academic papers. However, extracting and validating this information remains a major challenge due to inconsistent reporting formats, ambiguous variable definitions, and the need for manual interpretation. These issues introduce errors and significantly slow down the research process, particularly in metaanalyses of global poverty interventions. Accurate extraction of transfer amounts is especially important, yet papers report values in local currency (LCU), nominal USD (NUSD), or purchasing power parity (PPP), making manual validation timeconsuming and prone to human error. This project addresses these challenges by developing an AIassisted system to audit key financial variables in cash transfer studies. Using structured prompting and automated workflows, the system extracts planned transfer amounts directly from research papers and compares them to preexisting values stored in a centralized dataset. For any selected variable (xfer\_amt\_pln\_lcu, xfer\_amt\_pln\_nusd, or xfer\_amt\_pln\_ppp), the pipeline generates four subcolumns: the original spreadsheet value, the AIextracted value, a match/mismatch assessment, and the supporting quote from the paper. This structure enables systematic validation across studies and reduces reliance on manual verification. Developing this system required integrating AI coding agents, resolving Google authentication issues, and debugging cases where Codex returned incorrect values. Testing in the metadata audit sandbox demonstrates that the system reliably identifies agreement and disagreement between sources, highlighting both data inconsistencies and limitations in automated interpretation. By automating a previously manual and errorprone process, this project strengthens the reliability of transfer amount metadata and contributes to GPRL's broader effort to build scalable, AIassisted validation tools for development economics research.

Fingerprinting Carbon Capture: Tracing Enhanced Rock Weathering Through Soil with Strontium Isotopes and Alkalinity
Limiting global climate change requires not only reducing greenhouse gas emissions but also verifying carbon dioxide removal (CDR) strategies at statistically significant scales. Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) is a CDR strategy that accelerates the dissolution of silicate minerals in soils, converting atmospheric CO2 into stable aqueous alkalinity. As interest in ERW grows, accurately verifying carbon capture and distinguishing silicate-derived products from other sources has become a central challenge. Alkalinity measurements are widely used to quantify weathering-driven CO2 removal, but they are not source-specific and may reflect inputs from carbonates, fertilizers, or background soil processes. Current data show that basalt-amended systems produce elevated and stable alkalinity, with mean values of 28,940 3,020 mg/L compared to 25,480 2,870 mg/L in controls over a 13-month storage period, indicating minimal temporal variability; however, these measurements alone cannot confirm silicate-derived carbon capture. Combining radiogenic strontium isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) measured through a thermal ionization mass spectrometer with alkalinity measurements enables source-specific tracing of ERW processes through soil profiles. Depth-resolved analyses may reveal that basalt-amended soils exhibit distinct unradiogenic isotopic signatures alongside increased alkalinity, indicating mobilization of silicate-derived weathering products. Electrochromic devices (ECDs) are devices that change color and optical properties under an applied voltage and have widespread uses in smart windows, displays, and wearables. Typically, ECDs function through an electrochemical redox reaction, in which a change in voltage induces the transport of ions between the cathode and anode. An approach to overcome this limitation explores the use of structural color, in which color arises from the interaction of light with the nanoscale structures of particles. Structural color results from optical phenomena such as interference, diffraction, and scattering from nanostructures, allowing the color of light to be tuned by adjusting structural parameters such as interparticle spacing. Therefore, integrating structural color mechanisms into electrochromic architecture offers a promising pathway toward ECDs with a broader color palette. By incorporating nanostructures whose particle spacing can be electrically modulated into ECDs, it becomes possible to dynamically tune coloration across the continuous visible spectrum. Such systems have potential in expanding the functionality of ECDs for next-generation adaptive displays and optical technologies.

These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how policy reforms are implemented on the ground, examining how well-intentioned legislation can produce unintended consequences or inconsistencies in practice. Baseball's Highest Stakes Situation and a Decision Error Three Decades Deep
It's the bottom of the ninth inning, two outs, bases loaded. The conventional instinct in baseball is to swing at a hitter's count. This paper argues that instinct has been wrong for at least three decades and that the sport has not corrected it. With bases loaded and two outs, a walk simultaneously scores a run and preserves the identical threat for the next batter, who then faces the same high-leverage situation from a fresh count. This self-reinforcing property means that patience compounds across consecutive plate appearances in a way that attacking any individual pitch cannot match. This paper formalizes this using an augmented Markov Decision Process applied across 192 possible game states. The model recommends taking the pitch at 10 of 12 count states in a tied game and 11 of 12 when trailing by one run. Against 35 years of Major League Baseball pitch by pitch data, the gap between optimal and observed behavior is large and entirely unidirectional. Batters over-swing at every non-two-strike count, at costs reaching 19 percentage points of win probability at the single most expensive state. Not one of the 48 count-and-deficit combinations in the data shows under-swinging. The gap has not narrowed from 1990 to 2024, surviving the full analytics revolution. The finding connects to the behavioral economics literature on action bias and suggests that trained motor responses, unlike deliberate decisions, resist strategic correction.

However, once in power, this unstable foundation of manipulation causes flattery to be an ill-equipped substitute for the paranoia and death that Richard has caused. Simulating the Phase Behavior of Polydisperse DNA-Nanoparticle Systems

By manipulating PAE sizes and DNA sequences, the PAEs can form crystals with controllable lattice symmetry and nanoparticle spacing. The assembly of polydisperse PAE systems into a single phase has proven to be challenging due to the thermodynamic instability caused by size disparity. Recent experimental attempts have shown some success in single-phase crystallization by introducing flexible spacers within the DNAs to make the effective hydrodynamic radii more similar. However, it is unclear what the limits of the flexible spacers are in overcoming the effects of size disparity. Understanding the phase behavior requires systematic and quantitative analysis, which is extremely challenging experimentally due to the large number of systems that need to be synthesized and investigated. In this work, we construct a phase diagram of polydisperse PAE systems using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with two different models: a colloidal model and a coarse-grained DNA model. These models can provide crucial thermodynamic information with relatively low computational cost. The colloidal model is used to determine the boundaries of the phase diagram, while the coarse-grained model is used to explain any discrepancies with the experimental data and provide a detailed understanding of the thermodynamics of the interactions. In doing so, we explain the effects of nanoparticle core diameter, spacer flexibility, and nanoparticle type on crystallization, and provide guidelines for experimental synthesis.

Renaissance Mythological Afterlives: Transgressing Allusionary Bounds of the Lovers/Victims of Jove's Desire

This point of conflict leads to the emergence of a different form of female subjectivity that emphasizes transformation, both of speech and embodiment. This project presents a new framework for viewing female subjectivity in Renaissance drama that acknowledges these classical allusions not as mythological background noise, but as a foundational place where female embodiment emerges differently in literature and culture itself through a dialectical conversation with the classically-constrained past.

Race and Real Estate: Nathan William MacChesney and the Consequential Establishment of Northwestern's Streeterville Campus
This project examines the history of Northwestern University's medical schools' move to Streeterville in the 1920s and the enduring consequences for both the city's landscape and the institution's development. The relocation from the South Side was not merely logistical, but strategic, positioning Northwestern as a foundational presence in what became some of the most valuable real estate in Chicago. Using archives from the McCormick Library and the Chicago History Museum, this study uses Board of Trustees meeting minutes, correspondence involving the Chicago campus, published writings and addresses of MacChesney, and Sanborn fire insurance maps to trace the physical transformation of the Near North Side. MacChesney's role extended beyond university planning into developing restrictive covenants, private legal agreements used to enforce racial segregation, and eugenic thought and criminological institutions. Archival evidence indicates likely self-dealing in his promotion of University land purchases adjacent to his own property. The recent opening of a new Northwestern Medicine clinic in Bronzeville marks a return to the South Side, providing a contemporary moment to reflect on the origins and implications of this earlier move. By situating Northwestern's expansion within these broader systems, this project contributes to conversations about how institutions reckon with complex histories, highlighting the entanglement of educational growth, urban development, and racial inequality.

However, evidence that these gains translate to more accurate treatment effect estimation is lacking, revealing a disconnect between the tuning and evaluation stages. Sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and ROC curves were computed. Keypoint accuracy was calculated using Euclidean distance between ground truth and model detections. We analyzed 46 videos from 24 hospitalized patients with diverse racial backgrounds. OpenPose showed the highest AUC in 52% of cases (24/46) and highest overall balanced accuracy (BA) of 72% (53% sensitivity, 89% specificity). This research introduces a vesicular platform to enhance NK cell cytotoxicity and activity, as well as increase cancer cell lysis, by coupling cancer-specific activation and localized inhibition of CD16 cleavage, proposing a novel synthetic biology strategy to enhance NK cell-mediated cancer cell lysis.

How Children's Health Insurance Reduces Crime: The Role of Behavioral Health Services in Medicaid
The United States spends nearly $300 billion annually on the criminal justice system and $140 billion on children's Medicaid. Understanding whether childhood health insurance can reduce adulthood crime - and how - could reshape how policymakers think about both programs. This thesis investigates the mechanisms by which childhood Mediacid eligibility reduces adult criminal behavior. Using variation in state Medicaid eligibility rules across birth cohorts from 1981 to 1984, I estimate the effect of childhood health insurance access on adult arrest rates from FBI data. I then test three possible channels - improved education, reduced financial stress, and better access to behavioral health services - across national datasets covering education, income, mental health, and substance abuse treatment. Each additional year of childhood Medicaid eligibility substantially reduces adult drug and violent arrest rates, with the strongest effects emerging from eligibility during adolescence. Education and financial stress channels show largely insignificant results. Instead, the evidence points to behavioral health as the primary pathway where adolescent substance abuse treatment admissions roughly triple with each additional year of eligibility. These findings suggest that Medicaid reduces crime not by improving schooling or financial outcomes, but by connecting at-risk youth to mental health and substance abuse services during critical developmental windows. This points to Medicaid as both a health investment and a long-run public safety investment.

State Supreme Court Selection Mechanisms and Dissent

Potential New Regulators of Body Axis Formation in a Regenerating Marine Worm

Style Guide: Guiding the Institution and Beyond
The need for updated, student-centered style guides in journalism is increasingly important as reporting standards evolve across platforms, identities, and subject areas; under the guidance of my mentor, Elise K. As an emerging scholar, I approached this question by developing a structured database of existing style guides, organizing them into three categories: affinity-specific, medium-specific (such as photography and writing), and general or topic-specific guides. I analyzed each guide for accessibility, public availability, and relevance to current industry practices, while also documenting how guides reference and build upon one another. This process revealed that no style guide operates independently; instead, they are deeply interconnected, frequently drawing from shared language and frameworks, suggesting that institutional guides benefit from aligning with this larger body of work. The project also resulted in a comprehensive, organized record of these relationships and a system for tracking updates over time. Greenland's earliest ecosystems after the last glaciation: Younger Dryas and early Holocene leaf wax analysis
The Greenland Ice Sheet is shrinking due to anthropogenic climate change, which may dramatically alter ecosystem dynamics, especially in the Northern Hemisphere. During the last deglaciation 12,900 years ago, rapid melting of the Laurentide ice sheet abruptly reversed Earth's warming trend and returned northern regions to near-glacial conditions for over a thousand years. This event, termed the Younger Dryas (YD), is known for its severe temperature decrease, but less is known about its impacts on vegetation and hydrology. My project studies a Greenland lake sediment core spanning the last 13,000 years to analyze the environmental impacts of YD cooling. Lipid biomarkers from leaf waxes are well-preserved in lake sediments throughout time and are therefore used as records of the surrounding landscape. Leaf wax compositions are linked to vegetation source, productivity, and hydrology. Using these properties as paleoproxies, results show a sudden shift to an arid climate at the start of the YD, which stabilizes quickly to higher precipitation conditions after the YD termination. In contrast, regional vegetation productivity is low throughout the YD and is not reestablished until ~800 years post-YD, indicating a gradual landscape development to suitable growing conditions. This ~10.9 kya mark also displays a drastic vegetation turnover similar to a nearby lake which exhibits a shift from herb tundra to a more diverse dwarf shrub heath comparable to modern landscapes. Understanding these differing impacts and recovery timescales from the YD is crucial for contextualizing this extreme climate event in the view of current ice sheet loss.

Nitrogen-nitrogen bond formation via electrochemistry
Many clinically approved drugs contain N-N bonds. Yet, directly bonding two electron-rich nitrogen atoms defies the conventional reactivity pattern because most reactions take place between an electron-rich molecule (nucleophile) and an electron-deficient one (electrophile). For that reason, existing strategies for N-N bond formation often involve the formation of transient electron-deficient nitrogen intermediates. However, these approaches generally require at least one planar, sp2-hybridized nitrogen source. N-N coupling between two non-planar, sp3-hybridized nitrogen atoms is rare, with few reported examples and limited structural diversity. Additionally, these systems often undergo competing decomposition due to weak adjacent carbon-hydrogen bonds. This project employs electrochemistry to remove an electron (oxidize) from the nitrogen atom of a bicyclic compound known as quinuclidine, generating an sp3-hybridized nitrogen radical. Notably, quinuclidine radical avoids the typical decomposition pathway due to its structural constraints. The intermediate is also electrophilic, thereby overcoming the issue with polarity mismatch and reacting readily with nucleophilic nitrogen partners to form N-N bonds. Under the optimized electrochemical condition, oxidized quinuclidine couples with its electron-rich, unoxidized counterpart to produce a doubly positively charged N-N bonded dimer in high yield. This product can be further diversified through ring-opening reactions with oxygen-, nitrogen-, and sulfur-based reagents, providing access to a diverse set of highly functionalized molecules. Overall, this work provides a new route to medicinally relevant N(sp3)-N(sp3) bonded structures that have previously been difficult to synthesize.

Chemically Induced Dynein Relocalization in C. elegans Disrupts Faithful Meiosis
The formation of healthy egg (reproductive) cells depends on a special type of cell division called meiosis. During this process, cells build a structure called the spindle to separate chromosomes. Unlike most cells, egg cells lack typical organizing centers for this structure, making it less clear how the spindle forms and functions properly. This project focuses on dynein, a motor protein that helps move components within the cells along microtubules, which serve as tracks for chromosome movement. Because dynein is found in multiple parts of the spindle, we asked whether its function depends on where it is located. To test this, we use a system in the model organism C. elegans that allows us to artificially move dynein to a specific region, the spindle poles. We found that relocating dynein to the poles caused noticeable defects in cell division. In particular, cells showed misaligned chromosomes and failures in a key step called polar body extrusion. We also performed an embryonic lethality assay to assess the downstream effects of these defects and found significantly reduced embryo viability following dynein relocalization. Our findings suggest that dynein plays different roles depending on its position within the cell, and that disrupting its normal location interferes with proper cell division. By better understanding how proteins like dynein function in egg cells, this research may provide insight into the causes of chromosomal abnormalities and reproductive challenges.

"A snack is not a meal": Culture, Identity, and Dietary Change in Malawi
From KFC outlets in cities to freshly-fried potatoes in rural markets, Malawians have ever-increasing access to Westernized food options. Dominant frameworks for understanding dietary change predict an inevitable shift toward processed, unhealthy diets driven by income growth and urbanization. Without accounting for cultural nuances, however, such frameworks fail to capture uneven adoption of non-traditional ways of eating. Drawing on qualitative interviews, informal survey data and a historical analysis of Malawian food systems, this thesis proposes a four-part framework for understanding the social, cultural, and psychological dimensions through which Malawians navigate new food choices: financial pragmatism, competing heuristics of health and hygiene, the tension between tradition and novelty, and the weight of social perception. Central to this argument is the finding that a culturally specific distinction between a "snack" and a "real meal" functions as a mechanism of cultural appropriation, allowing Malawians to integrate Western food into their lives while maintaining a linguistic and conceptual separation from traditional eating habits. Furthermore, interviews reveal hygiene concerns are circumvented through brand-name heuristics and community-built online approval; health knowledge does not straightforwardly determine behavior; and status functions as an external enforcement mechanism which, unlike tradition, does not uniformly push against Western food but cuts in contradictory directions depending on context, generation, and the type of food involved. Together, these findings challenge homogenization narratives and call for food policy that engages not only with nutritional and economic dimensions, but with the cultural logic of eating.

Women Between Worlds: American Wives as Cultural Ambassadors in Meiji Japan
This research examines the role of American women in Meiji Japan as participants in cross-cultural exchange during a period of rapid political and social transformation. The research takes the form of a history thesis focused on Emma Wigmore, Mary Crawford Fraser, and Mary McNeill Fenollosa, who all traveled to Japan as the wives of foreign diplomats and hired professionals. It argues that expatriate wives functioned as informal, two-way cultural ambassadors who mediated between Japanese and American societies. Drawing on letters, diaries, and published writings as the primary source materials, this study foregrounds the experiences of three women to show how they interpreted Japanese culture for audiences at home while simultaneously introducing Euro-American customs into the spaces they occupied in Japan. The thesis situates these experiences within the broader context of Japan's efforts to renegotiate unequal treaties and assert its status as a modern nation in the late nineteenth century. As foreign diplomats, educators, and technical experts established communities in cities such as Yokohama and Tokyo, women became embedded in the social and domestic networks that sustained cross-cultural interaction in Japan. They engaged with Japanese people and culture by hosting gatherings, forming friendships, traveling, collecting material goods, and writing. This thesis demonstrates that by the end of the 1890s, these women were actively immersing themselves in Japanese society and producing knowledge about the country through published writings. This study expands the scope of diplomatic history during the Meiji Period and underscores the importance of women's experiences during this era.

From the Atlantic to the Lakeshore: Practicing Samba and Constructing Brasilidade in Chicago
This sociological study explores how samba practitioners in Chicago teach, discuss, and perform samba as an Afro-Brazilian music and dance practice, and how this relates to race, nationalism, and identity in Brazil. While there is extensive scholarship on samba in Brazil, there is much less on samba outside Brazil, and in U.S. Latine studies and immigration studies Brazilians are understudied. There are a few older studies on one Chicago samba group but none on the current small, passionate, and interconnected scene. Motivated by my experiences attending Chicago samba events and interest in racialization, diaspora, and music related to Latin Americans in the U.S., including Brazilians, this study relies on semi-structured interviews with samba teachers and leaders from 7 organizations, as well as participant observations of samba classes and events. A transnational approach ties the data's emergent themes to ethnographies on samba in Brazil, as well as postcolonial and Movimento Negro scholarship. This study is ongoing, but early analysis indicates that a few key Afro-Brazilian leaders trained the majority of Chicago's samba dance teachers, resulting in a number of programs that forefront Afro-Brazilian history in their pedagogy, with some exceptions. They recruit new participants, primarily non-Brazilian and some Brazilians, through appeals to broad interest in Latin dance and festivities. To varying extents, samba organizations in Chicago perform samba as a form of Black diasporic resistance Chicagoans can join or learn about, as familiar national culture Brazilian immigrants can reconnect with, or as spectacle non-Brazilians can consume.

Storytelling & Video Editing for Protest Tradition: The NBA Bubble Podcast
In the summer of 2020, the NBA created a biosecure "bubble" at Disney World to finish its season amidst a global pandemic. Though often glazed over as a health, athletic, and financial success, this project examines the bubble's reckoning with the pandemic and the Black Lives Matter movement to reevaluate the practice of protest in sports. The podcast further examines the tension between athletes' economic privilege and their inextricable Blackness, asking whether proximity to wealth severs or deepens connections within communities most harmed by racial violence. Effort was dedicated to making the content accessible for all listeners to amplify the impact of sports' role in politics and calls for justice. This podcast asks who controlled the bubble, and to what end, challenging listeners to reflect on their own social values, expectations of athletes, and the opportunities for progress spurred by protest in sports.

Using Bio-compatible Conductive Hydrogels for On-Demand Drug Delivery
Liposomes, which are tiny spherical capsules made of the same material as cell membranes, have emerged as a promising platform for delivering chemotherapy drugs directly to solid tumors like breast and ovarian cancers. By encapsulating the drugs in these biocompatible spheres, researchers have made progress in protecting them from rapid clearance in the blood, something that has long limited the effectiveness of cancer treatments. However, the drugs are still cleared away from the tumor site too quickly to provide localized, long-lasting delivery. Hydrogels, which are water-swollen polymer networks similar in texture to soft tissue, offer a promising next step as encapsulated drugs are released slowly as the hydrogel is broken down by the body. Since the drug release rate depends on the mechanical properties of the hydrogel it is difficult to optimize. Our proposed solution to this issue involves creating conductive hydrogels that could release the encapsulated drugs on demand when an electrical signal is applied. This would allow for adaptive drug delivery, optimized to the patient's needs. To build this platform, we incorporated a conductive polymer called S-PEDOT into a sodium alginate hydrogel. We have already confirmed that our hydrogels have mechanical properties comparable to biological tissue and identified an optimal polymer composition that maximizes conductivity. The next step is loading these gels with drug-filled liposomes and demonstrating voltage-triggered release. This platform, which has not been previously reported in the literature, could ultimately enable precise, on-demand delivery of cancer drugs directly to solid tumor sites.

Foreclosure to Financialization: Mapping Institutional Investor Penetration in SingleFamily Housing Markets After 2008
For many aspiring first-time homebuyers, the single-family home has shifted from a pathway to stability to a restricted financial asset, shaped in part by the post-2008 rise of institutional investors in the single-family rental market. Drawing on CoreLogic property-level data, the study constructs a longitudinal spatial dataset across three metropolitan areas [Atlanta, Charlotte, and Jacksonville] using kernel density estimation, spatial autocorrelation analysis, and demographic overlays to trace changes from a pre-investor baseline (2009) through a pre-COVID snapshot (2019) to the present (2025). In Charlotte, high-investor tracts have median incomes 48% lower and Black population shares five times greater than low-investor tracts, consistent with investor targeting of historically distressed, minority-majority neighborhoods. Together, these patterns suggest institutional investor activity represents a durable structural transformation rather than a temporary crisis response. By mapping institutional portfolio intersections with historically accessible ownership opportunities, this project contributes to debates about financialization, intergenerational wealth-building, and housing equity. The evidence suggests institutional investors have reshaped the single-family market by concentrating ownership in distressed communities, reducing first-time buyer access to homeownership.

However, emerging evidence has identified distinct GPe neuron populations based on molecular identity, axonal targets, and behavioral impacts, suggesting that the GPe's contributions to motor control extends beyond a single relay pathway. We observed projections to multiple motor-related regions, including the dorsal striatum, cortex, GPi, substantia nigra (pars reticulata and compacta), subthalamic nucleus, pedunculopontine nucleus, and olivary nuclei. Together, these findings demonstrate that Npas1+ GPe neurons participate in a distributed network rather than a single STN-mediated pathway, refining models of basal ganglia function and providing insight into how disruptions in GPe connectivity contribute to motor dysfunction in disorders such as Parkinson's disease.

@DarkHumor: Race-Blindness, Racism, and Racialization in Mexican Digital Discourse
The ideology of mestizaje, which touts the development of an exceptional “raceless” race through centuries of racial mixture in Latin America, is a core component of the Mexican identity. However, racism remains a central facet of Mexico’s landscape, perpetuating the erasure and subjugation of the Black, Indigenous, and Asian presence and experiences in the country’s national identity. Despite claiming unity, mestizaje sustains the race-blind conditions needed to ignore, deny, and disavow racism in Mexico. The public nature of social media can provide important insights into the process of racialization by providing an accessible view of popular reactions to racism. Digital satirical environments are rife with racist language, made permissible under the guise of dark humor. The novelty of digital social network research, coupled with the recency of the 2024 presidential elections, signal an opportunity to address understudied phenomena. I focus on a racist political post by popular Mexican meme account @EsDeMamador on X (previously Twitter) on the day of the election. I utilize an intersectional framework to analyze an array of 56 pre-selected (sub)replies to the original post. Drawing from literature on ethics in the digital humanities, Critical and Computer-Mediated Discourse Analysis, post-colonialism, and Critical Race Theory, I illuminate how non-racial categories (i.e., class, political party, religion) are weaponized as instruments of racialization. These reflect, refract, and advance exclusionary national imaginaries. My findings accentuate how white supremacy, anti-Blackness, and anti-Indigeneity continue to permeate daily interactions in Mexico today, despite the country’s alignment with race-blind ideologies.

A Deep Learning-Based Segmentation Model for Epithelial Cells Infected with Listeria monocytogenes
Accurate detection of objects from microscopy images, otherwise known as segmentation, is a necessary and limiting first step in quantifying cellular responses. In recent years, this process has been automated using tools such as Cellpose, which rely on neural networks trained on images with cytoplasmic or whole-cell fluorescence signal to segment cell borders. However, in multiplexed imaging approaches, this is challenging as there may not be enough channels to dedicate to segmentation. My project aims to evaluate whether I could use the biosensor signals, which vary between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, to develop a model to identify the borders of epithelial cells infected with the bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. To do this, I developed a computational pipeline to integrate the generalized segmentation model Cellpose-SAM with biosensor images from infected cells. As expected, basic Cellpose models were found to be unable to identify the borders of epithelial cells, preferring to segment the nucleus. I trained a model on manually annotated biosensor images and evaluated it using a standard metric, Intersection over Union. The trained model was able to identify the varied cytoplasmic signals from the biosensors, allowing for better segmentation of epithelial cell borders. To evaluate the utility of the model, I compared the results with those obtained using the Voronoi diagram, a commonly employed method for identifying cell borders in an epithelium. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing deep learning models for the segmentation of biosensor data, the identification of infected cells, and the quantification of bacterial load.

Experiences of Racial Mismatch and Relationship to Racial Belonging
